documents.abstract: Abstract Public discussions about whether artificial intelligence possesses emotions, subjective experience, or even consciousness often rely on linguistic output, behavioral performance, and observers’ judgments. An AI system’s ability to describe its own state is not, by itself, sufficient to demonstrate subjective experience. At the same time, the fact that an AI system is non-biological does not by itself justify the conclusion that it lacks all forms of subjective experience. This paper proposes a cross-system experimental framework. When humans and artificial intelligence systems are exposed to functionally corresponding external stimuli, researchers can record brain activity in humans and internal states in AI systems, then compare how the stimuli alter internal processing and how those changes affect subsequent judgments and behavior. The goal is not to require AI systems to reproduce the structure, waveforms, or numerical values of the human brain, but to identify response relationships that can survive repeated testing and causal examination. Such comparison cannot be achieved merely by converting two kinds of data into the same format. Researchers must first establish what candidate measures mean within each system, then construct possible cross-system correspondences and test whether those correspondences can predict changes under new materials and new conditions. Only when a proposed relationship does more than describe existing results, and instead generates successful new predictions, is there stronger reason to discuss whether the two systems may share some common processing principle. Using “violation of an acquired expectation” as an example, this paper illustrates how the framework could be translated into an initial research program. It also distinguishes transient computational states, states maintained within context, and persistent states across sessions, and discusses long-term interaction, consciousness-relevant human controls, internal intervention, and statistical confounds. This paper is a conceptual and methodological proposal. It does not provide an already validated test for consciousness, nor does it claim to have solved all technical problems of cross-system comparison. Even if the results ultimately fail to support the presence of subjective experience in artificial intelligence, data linking external conditions, internal states, and subsequent behavior may still be useful for model evaluation, training, and interaction design.

Deep learning-based IoT botnet detection has reached high predictive performance; however, its practical deployment remains constrained by the lack of operationally actionable explainability. This paper introduces TimeAnchor, a hybrid explainability framework that integrates TimeSHAP and Anchors to enhance the temporal stability and internal consistency of explanations while preserving acceptable fidelity. The approach is evaluated on two complementary datasets: CICIDS2017, reflecting controlled and structured traffic conditions, and IoT-23, characterised by real-world, noisy, and highly heterogeneous attack scenarios. The results indicate that TimeAnchor substantially improves explanation consistency and stability across both corpora, achieving high coherence on CICIDS2017 and yielding average gains in stability and consistency on IoT-23 compared with the individual methods. These improvements are accompanied by a moderate trade-off in local fidelity, which appears acceptable given the overall enhancement in explanatory robustness. These findings support the relevance of TimeAnchor for explainable IoT botnet detection in dynamic and realistic operational environments.
topics: Internet Traffic Analysis and Secure E-voting

documents.abstract: In an era defined by intensifying uncertainties, spanning geopolitical tensions, climate variability, pandemics and global supply chain disruption, fuzzy multi-criteria decision-making (FMCDM) has emerged as a critical paradigm for robust risk assessment and mitigation. This chapter presents a comprehensive review of recent advances in FMCDM from 2021 to 2025, synthesizing insights from over 400 studies across sectors such as healthcare, engineering and sustainable operations. Key developments include the rapid growth of hybrid fuzzy models integrating interval type-2 fuzzy sets with methods like TOPSIS, DEMATEL and BWM, as well as the evolution of enriched fuzzy extensions (e.g., Fermatean and T-spherical sets) to address complex, multi-dimensional vagueness. Persistent issues such as computational scalability, inconsistencies in expert judgements and the challenges of modelling epistemic uncertainty are critically examined. Empirical evidence highlights applications such as fuzzy-enhanced healthcare risk matrices, which improve transparency by up to 30% through probabilistic membership functions. The chapter identifies emerging directions involving the fusion of FMCDM with artificial intelligence, machine learning, big-data analytics and blockchain to enable real-time, adaptive and secure decision environments. By bridging theoretical advancements with practical implementations, this chapter offers actionable insights for designing resilient, uncertainty-aware risk governance frameworks in an increasingly volatile global context.

The evolution of medical tourism is increasingly characterised by a shift from isolated, procedure-based journeys to complex, transnational care pathways supported by digital innovation and changing patient values. As technological advances—including genomics, artificial intelligence, and telemedicine—reshape the organisation of care, the industry faces a dual challenge: harnessing innovation to improve patient outcomes while addressing urgent concerns about equity, sustainability, and data governance. This chapter explores the future trends and systemic challenges shaping the next phase of cross-border care. It examines the rise of personalised and precision medicine, highlighting how genomic testing and targeted therapies enable customised treatment while raising new ethical questions. It considers the rapid expansion of wellness and mental health tourism, emphasising evidence-based, integrative models that balance clinical rigour with environmental sustainability. A central focus is digital infrastructure and trust—assessing how AI, remote monitoring, and blockchain can create safer, “tele-first” pathways that lower carbon footprints and enhance continuity of care. By addressing fragmented accountability and the risk of widening health inequalities, the chapter concludes that the future of medical tourism depends on a value-driven approach where destinations differentiate themselves through transparency, ethical governance, and a genuine commitment to the well-being of both patients and local communities.

Document annotation is a fundamental yet labor-intensive step in building document information extraction systems. While Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Large Language Models (LLMs) can automate parts of this process, we argue that annotation systems should be judged not by how completely they remove human effort, but by how effectively they redirect it toward review and correction. We propose a modular human-in-the-loop architecture that integrates OCR-based extraction, LLM-based semantic pre-annotation, and human validation in a single editable workflow, and present \textbf{GAIDA}, a research prototype serving as its reference implementation. GAIDA supports interchangeable OCR engines, LLM backends, and prompt configurations, and enables stage-specific measurement of annotation effort. In an initial single-annotator, stage-specific study on the FUNSD scanned-form and WildReceipt retail-receipt benchmarks, OCR assistance reduced region-creation and transcription time by up to \textbf{80.9\%}, and reviewing LLM pre-annotations reduced semantic-labeling time by up to \textbf{73.7\%}, despite imperfect pre-annotations of 78.86\% and 86.98\% Micro F1 on FUNSD and WildReceipt, respectively. Finally, we reuse the same implementation, adapting only OCR and prompt configuration, to build and openly release \textbf{AraReceipt}, a manually annotated dataset of 100 Arabic receipt images labeled with 25 key-information classes. The results indicate that imperfect automated outputs provide practical value when presented as editable suggestions under human control.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into game-based learning (GBL) offers adaptive, personalized, and engaging experiences for early language education. AI-powered games can enhance vocabulary, listening comprehension, and speaking confidence through real-time feedback and adaptive difficulty, but raise questions about balancing AI guidance, parental involvement, and child autonomy. Drawing on GBL theory, flow theory, and the input hypothesis, this paper identifies four dimensions of balance—pedagogical, parental involvement, engagement, and child autonomy—and proposes research questions and a conceptual framework for AI-supported game-based microlearning systems for English acquisition among children aged 5–8.

Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to learn new classes continuously without forgetting the previously learned ones. Recent works in CIL have significantly advanced across various modalities; however, at the intersection of audio-visual modality, this problem remains underexplored. While representations from multimodal foundational models (MFMs) encapsulate rich static priors, our preliminary analysis shows that these representations struggle in incremental settings. Motivated by this, we propose a framework that generalizes frozen MFMs to audio-visual CIL. Specifically, we leverage their dense audio and visual representations and employ an attention-based contextual guidance module, in which the audio representations serve as task-stable contextual guidance for the visual representations, enabling effective class recognition in the incremental setting. To further mitigate catastrophic forgetting and preserve stability across tasks, we employ feature- and logit-level distillation, which are primarily responsible for the reduced forgetting. Extensive evaluations across various audio-visual CIL benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Code is available at https://github.com/avigupta2798/MFM-CIL.

documents.abstract: The study draws on two complementary data sources. The quantitative data come from a cross-sectional online survey administered to university students enrolled in Turkish higher education institutions. Stratified random sampling ensures representation across institutional types. The strata include metropolitan foundation universities, metropolitan public universities, and provincial state universities. The survey instrument uses validated scales adapted from prior research on Technology Continuance Theory and GenAI adoption. All items are measured on a five-point Likert scale. The constructs measured include Perceived Ease of Use, Perceived Usefulness, Confirmation, Satisfaction, Trust, Perceived Security, Continuance Intention, and Use. Trust items measure confidence in the AI tools. One item asks whether students trust GenAI tools to provide accurate information. Another asks whether students trust developers to prevent unethical use of student data. The survey does not measure trust in university administration. The survey is available in Turkish and English. Translation follows a rigorous protocol. The research team drafts the survey in English, translates it into Turkish, and back-translates it into English. Native speakers review both versions for clarity, cultural accuracy, and linguistic equivalence.The qualitative data come from semi-structured interviews with academics. Purposive sampling recruits academics across three institutional strata. The strata are elite foundation universities in Istanbul, major public universities in Ankara, and provincial state universities in eastern and southeastern Türkiye. The sample also includes academics from Northern Cyprus, transnational institutions, and the Turkish and Kurdish diaspora. The interview protocol explores GenAI use in teaching and research, perceptions of institutional support, experiences with infrastructure limitations, views on domestic AI models, and intentions regarding academic migration. The protocol includes specific probes for Kurdish academics and academics at conservative foundation universities. The interview guide is drafted in English and translated into Turkish and Kurdish. Native speakers review both translations. Back-translation ensures linguistic equivalence. Interviews are conducted in Turkish, Kurdish, or English based on participant preference. Interviews are audio-recorded with participant consent and transcribed verbatim.Data analysis uses Generalized Structured Component Analysis in SmartPLS 4.0 for the quantitative phase. Preliminary data screening uses SPSS 28. Screening includes tests for normality, multicollinearity, and common method bias. The qualitative phase uses WEBQDA for digital coding. The coding framework includes deductive codes from Technology Continuance Theory and inductive codes that emerge from the data. Deductive codes include Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, Satisfaction, Trust in AI tools, Perceived Security, and Continuance Intention. Inductive codes include Institutional Trust, Infrastructure Context, Diaspora and Academic Retention, and Domestic AI Sovereignty. The research team builds a code co-occurrence matrix to trace links between institutional trust and trust in AI tools.Ethical approval comes from the Ethics Committee of CEOS.PP at the Polytechnic Institute of Porto. Data collection follows the Turkish Personal Data Protection Law and the General Data Protection Regulation. Participants receive information sheets and provide written informed consent. All data are anonymised upon collection. Participants receive alphanumeric codes that indicate region and institutional type but do not reveal individual identities. Audio recordings are deleted after transcription. Transcripts are stored on an encrypted, password-protected server accessible only to the research team. Data are retained for five years and then permanently deleted.

Advances in generative AI are opening new opportunities for mathematics learning in higher education, but systematic mapping of the Theory–Context–Methodology (TCM) framework to integrate generative AI into mathematics learning remains limited. This study aims to identify the theories or conceptual frameworks, application contexts, and research methods used in studies of generative AI in higher education mathematics education. The method used is a PRISMA-based systematic literature review. The search was conducted on Scopus, Lens, and Dimensions, yielding 322 initial articles; after deduplication, screening, and eligibility assessment, 31 articles were analyzed. Article quality was assessed using the MMAT, while data were analyzed through TCM-based coding. The results indicate that generative AI is conceptualized as a pedagogical tool, a technology adoption, pedagogical competence, mathematical activity, and a cognitive partner. Its application is dominant in the classroom, general mathematics, ChatGPT, and for conceptual understanding. Methodologically, the studies were dominated by qualitative and quantitative approaches, while mixed methods and R&D/development research remained limited. These findings underscore the need for AI-based instructional designs that are critical, ethical, and supported by more integrative empirical research.

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models in Higher Education: Applications, Challenges, Ethical Concerns, and Future Directions explores the growing role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) in transforming higher education. The book examines their applications in teaching, learning, research, academic writing, assessment, and personalized education. It highlights how AI-powered tools can support educators, enhance student engagement, improve access to learning resources, and facilitate academic productivity. At the same time, it addresses key challenges, including academic dishonesty, data privacy, algorithmic bias, misinformation, and the potential overdependence on AI-generated content. The book also discusses ethical considerations, institutional policies, responsible AI use, and the importance of maintaining human judgment in educational practices. Furthermore, it explores future directions, emerging technologies, and strategies for integrating AI into higher education effectively. This book is a valuable resource for educators, researchers, students, academic administrators, and policymakers interested in understanding and responsibly adopting AI-driven educational innovations.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) recently appeared as an issue of its time which has been changing the educational landscape at a considerable rate and opening new pathways and challenges for educators and learners. Therefore, in terms of GenAI for education this bibliometric analysis will characterize the change and development by mapping trends and patterns, examining prevalent subject areas in academia interest. Following the established criteria, we ran a systematic search on Scopus database with the identification and analysis of 121 peer-reviewed documents (journal articles, review articles and conference papers; selection reported with reference to the PRISMA 2020 guideline) published between January 2023 and March 2025 related to GenAI applied in education. The thematic labels attached to the algorithmically generated VOSviewer clusters were assigned by the researchers, and interpretations of regional patterns are presented as tentative. The article features papers discussing ways to use GenAI in learner-centered teaching, curriculum development and assessment. The findings reveal a rapid increase in research output between 2023 (23 articles) and 2024 (67 articles), followed by 31 articles in the first quarter of 2025, and substantial international collaboration (34% of the articles). Moreover, the thematic analysis shows that pedagogical integration and instructional design (55.4% of the articles), assessment and academic integrity (44.6%) and ethical and societal implications (39.7%) are the most prominent themes, with a shift from ethical and assessment concerns in 2023 towards pedagogical integration and learning outcomes in 2024-2025. Research affiliated with the United States, the United Kingdom, China and Germany dominates the corpus, whereas research from Latin America and Africa appears under-represented. The review proposes future directions of research and spells out an array of issues that have until now gone unexamined by helping the reader enter the intellectual landscape of GenAI in education. The bibliometric evidence indicates growing scholarly attention to the potential of GenAI in education; this study did not appraise the quality of the evidence on learning outcomes. Nonetheless, designers are being asked to collectively conduct further research to address any potential negative effects of the technology, and create useful design frameworks, to implement this technology into the education system worldwide, without compromising on justice and morality.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming language and literary studies by introducing new approaches to language learning, writing, translation, textual interpretation, literary analysis, and creative production. Powered by large language models and other generative technologies, these systems can generate and revise texts, summarize complex literary works, identify linguistic patterns, support multilingual communication, and facilitate interactive learning. However, their growing adoption raises important concerns regarding authorship, academic integrity, linguistic bias, cultural representation, interpretive reliability, data privacy, and the potential marginalization of less-resourced languages and literary traditions. This systematic review examines the applications, ethical challenges, and future directions of GenAI in language and literary studies. It adopts a structured literature-review approach to synthesize research on educational applications, computational linguistics, translation, literary interpretation, creative writing, and digital humanities. The review organizes the literature around five major themes: language learning and teaching, academic and creative writing, translation and multilingual communication, literary analysis and interpretation, and ethical and institutional governance. The synthesis suggests that GenAI can expand access to language-learning support, facilitate text-based research, improve writing processes, and support new forms of literary experimentation. Nevertheless, its effectiveness depends on human oversight, contextual accuracy, critical evaluation, and sensitivity to linguistic and cultural diversity. The review further identifies continuing challenges associated with fabricated information, algorithmic bias, unclear intellectual-property arrangements, overreliance on automated assistance, and inadequate representation of minority languages. It argues that GenAI should complement rather than replace human linguistic judgment, literary expertise, and creative agency. Future research should prioritize transparent evaluation frameworks, culturally responsive models, multilingual equity, responsible pedagogical integration, and interdisciplinary collaboration. The review contributes an integrated perspective for researchers, educators, writers, and institutions seeking to use generative technologies responsibly in language and literary scholarship.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Explicit ratio prompts can request intermediate writing styles, but endpoint classification does not reveal proportional responses at internal ratios. We present a geometric protocol using model-specific endpoints and shared references in external sentence-embedding spaces. It excludes mechanically perfect endpoints from primary errors, retains unclipped projections, and separates axial calibration error from normalized off-axis drift. StyleBlend-Bench contains eight style axes and 320 scenarios. Five Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 checkpoints generated 33,600 texts over seven ratios and three seeds; three encoders produced 100,800 geometric records. An external GPT generator adds 6719 usable texts. A full five-model prompt-by-temperature experiment contains 95,994 usable condition records. Shared-reference BGE-M3 calibration error ranges from 0.176 to 0.212; other encoder/reference choices change model ordering. Two automatic evaluators correlate strongly in style intensity (r = 0.910), but content-pass agreement is 76.2%. The trajectories were rarely one-dimensional: first-component variance ranged from 0.349 to 0.408 and ordered path-length ratios from 4.64 to 5.20. The protocol diagnoses model response under specified anchors and encoders; it does not establish a human perceptual scale or absolute cross-model style coordinate.

Training foundation models at the frontier typically requires large-scale dedicated and centralized clusters with fast interconnects - infrastructure that is prohibitively expensive and generally accessible only to well-resourced organizations. Decentralized training over pooled, geographically distributed GPUs offers an alternative, but introduces substantial heterogeneity in compute, memory, power, and network performance. Existing distributed training systems are primarily designed for clusters with fast, low-latency interconnects and typically use all available GPUs when configuring parallel training. In geo-distributed environments, however, slower devices and weak network links can become bottlenecks, while optimizing solely for throughput overlooks significant energy cost. We present GeoTrain, an automatic parallelism system that jointly optimizes training performance and energy consumption for heterogeneous geo-distributed GPU environments. GeoTrain simultaneously selects GPUs, partitions model layers, and determines pipeline configurations while accounting for heterogeneous compute, memory, power, and network constraints. To efficiently explore this large combinatorial search space, GeoTrain employs an optimized memetic algorithm with specialized genetic operators and local search. Experiments with decoder-only Transformer models on real-world and simulated heterogeneous topologies demonstrate that GeoTrain reduces iteration time and energy consumption by up to $61.4\%$ and $11.7\%$, respectively, over the existing state-of-the-art approaches. It also finds the exact optimum on verifiable instances and scales beyond exact methods as the number of GPUs increases, while exposing favorable energy-time trade-offs, including cases where its time-optimal distributed training plan is both faster and more energy-efficient than the baselines.

Research Software Engineering (RSEng) is grounded in the belief that better, higher-quality software enables better research. As we look to the future of RSEng, we see that generative AI could substantially accelerate and expand the scope of research software development, but it also fundamentally shifts the nature of research software development by making code easier to generate than to understand, validate, or maintain. This is especially consequential in scientific computing, where software quality is directly tied to reproducibility, trust, and scientific validity. For RSEs, there is now an urgent need to advance a practical vision for how we will succeed in producing high-quality, trustworthy software under these new circumstances. We argue that in the age of AI for science, developers play an essential role in creating quality by reasoning about, negotiating, and ensuring it across the software lifecycle. We advance a theory that helps explain what, exactly, developers contribute by focusing on three constructs: values, which shape which quality attributes matter; expertise, which enables individuals to pursue and evaluate those attributes; and collaboration, which coordinates diverse forms of knowledge and accountability. To both build better AI tools for research software development and prepare our workforce, we need to better understand which values, what kinds of expertise, and what forms of collaboration will prove most helpful. For that, we seek expert input from Research Software Engineers(RSEs). This poster provides participants with an entertaining, interactive experience with the core ideas of our research. As well as sharing the preliminary thoughts and opinions gathered from an interview study that is currently underway. This interview study was motivated by the work this poster is highlighting. By showing the preliminary results we hope to initiate a dialog with RSEs. As such invite the audience to reflect on what quality means in their own practice, and the work that is needed to achieve it in concert with AI. Attendees can contribute responses on post-it notes attached to the poster and will be invited to continue the conversation through a survey. We will encourage those who wish to learn more about our team’s ongoing work on these topics to attend our talk "We Create Quality: Towards a Human-Centric Theory of Research Software Quality in the Age of AI”.

Purpose This study aims to map global research trends in aged care facilities management (ACFM) and identify thematic gaps to inform future practice and policy. Design/methodology/approach A scoping review and bibliometric analysis were conducted using the Scopus database, extracting 454 peer-reviewed articles (1980–2024) from 173 journals. The review followed preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, while VOSviewer and Biblioshiny were applied to analyse co-authorship, co-citation, keyword networks and thematic evolution. Findings Three thematic clusters dominate the field: assistive technologies for digital health monitoring, safety and autonomy; integrated care systems embedded in physical environments to deliver person-centred services; and community-based infrastructures that support ageing-in-place. Despite growth in publications, gaps remain in linking facilities management with sociotechnical and gerontological perspectives, limiting integration of digital innovations and interdisciplinary frameworks. Practical implications The findings highlight actionable strategies for policymakers, designers and facility managers to integrate technology, spatial design and community services, enabling more inclusive and resilient aged care environments. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first combined scoping review and bibliometric analysis of ACFM. It positions facilities management (FM) as a critical driver in addressing ageing challenges and advancing inclusive, technology-enabled care.

documents.abstract: Large language models are deployed globally, yet safety alignment and evaluation remain concentrated in English: harmful requests refused in English can elicit unsafe completions when translated into low-resource languages. We evaluate ten widely deployed LLMs across 79 languages (English plus 78 low-resource) under a translation-bypass threat model, using a metric conditioned on English safety, which separates translation bypass from unsafety already present in English. English safety does not transfer reliably: conditioned on safe English completions, mean bypass rates range from 21.9% to 44.4%. Bypass risk concentrates in a subset of language families, a pattern broadly shared across models. The shared ordering is confounded with translation degeneracy, but its variation across models is significant and survives every control we apply. We also show that per-model bypass rates do not identify a stable ranking: nine of ten models change rank across three conditioning schemes that estimate the same quantity, with no change to any underlying response.

documents.abstract: This study aims to analyze the development, research trends, and intellectual structure of health service innovation in public sector organizations through a comprehensive bibliometric approach. This investigation is particularly timely in response to the escalating global demand for effective healthcare delivery and the transformative impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on institutional frameworks. Despite the rapidly growing body of literature concerning public health management, comprehensive bibliometric studies that systematically map the specific intersection of "innovation" and "public sector healthcare" remain notably limited. To address this gap, this study employs a quantitative bibliometric methodology, analyzing 379 high-quality documents retrieved from the Scopus database after a rigorous multi-stage filtering process to ensure data relevance and academic rigor. The analytical framework combines performance analysis with advanced science mapping techniques, including co-occurrence (co-word) analysis and bibliographic coupling. VOSviewer software was utilized for network visualization and thematic clustering to identify the underlying intellectual linkages. The results demonstrate a significant and exponential increase in publications after 2019, underscoring a shift in global research priorities. Dominant keywords identified include telemedicine, human factors, healthcare delivery systems, and public hospital management. The analysis further delineates four key thematic clusters: digital health transformation, clinical and demographic studies, public healthcare service optimization, and pandemic-driven crisis innovation. These findings highlight the critical role of COVID-19 as a catalyst in accelerating the adoption of disruptive technologies. The study emphasizes that for public sector organizations to remain resilient, there is an urgent need to strengthen digital health infrastructure and implement adaptive governance models that can accommodate rapid technological shifts. Ultimately, this research provides a structured mapping of thematic evolution and intellectual linkages, offering a strategic roadmap for policymakers and scholars to identify under-researched areas and prioritize future interventions in health service innovation.

Recent advances in multimodal models have enabled GPT-6 Astra to perform robotic manipulation through in-context learning. Yet contact-rich control and tactile perception are often regarded as strengths of specialist policies, leaving open whether Astra can directly understand and use tactile observations. We provide, to our knowledge, the first demonstration that Astra directly interprets vision-based tactile images and uses their contact cues for manipulation. Tactile RGB images enter through its existing visual interface, enabling few-shot closed-loop control on nineteen simulated UniVTAC and OpenViTac tasks with 210 sampled scene seeds per setting. With visuo-tactile input, Astra achieves mean success rates of 93.8% and 81.8%, exceeding the strongest reported specialist baselines in our comparison by 22.9 and 13.1 percentage points, respectively. Vision-only performance also leads these baselines, reaching 76.3% and 80.6%. Trajectory analysis reveals active probing, cautious grasping, contact-guided alignment, and recovery, alongside difficulties with tangential loading and corrective execution. Our findings challenge the exclusivity of specialist policies in contact-rich manipulation and show that fine-grained vision can partially compensate for missing touch. They also identify vision-based tactile sensing as an interface for scaling contact understanding with foundation models and reveal signs of benchmark saturation. These results motivate joint visual-tactile pretraining, harder contact-rich evaluations, and physical-robot validation.

The rapid evolution of Large Language Models is fueled by massive datasets, yet this reliance poses severe privacy risks, as models can inadvertently memorize and even directly output sensitive training data. Synthetic text generation offers a promising solution to this challenge; however, existing methods struggle to reconcile rigorous privacy guarantees with high data utility. In this paper, we propose a new paradigm for private synthetic text generation: Guided Diffusion. Leveraging the unique steerability of Diffusion Language Models, we introduce novel sampling and re-masking procedures that actively guide the iterative denoising steps. These mechanisms steer the generative process to reconstruct fluent text that adheres to a target semantic distribution. We demonstrate that our framework is naturally compatible with Differential Privacy (DP): once the semantic embeddings of the private corpus are protected, the DP guarantee carries over to the generated text by post-processing. Empirically, we show that our approach generates high-quality synthetic text with precise semantic alignment. Furthermore, we validate its effectiveness in DP synthetic text generation: across two datasets and two diffusion backbones, it outperforms Private Evolution and DP-SGD-based fine-tuning in distributional fidelity and downstream utility, while generating significantly faster than Private Evolution. We further extend the framework to Data-Specific Indistinguishability (DSI), which adds a formal certificate against data poisoning and memorization at a small utility cost.

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Healthcare workforce health and well-being are explicitly included within the Health Promoting Hospitals and Health Services (HPH&HS) framework, but the literature has not been synthesized through a dedicated workforce-centered lens. This narrative review examined how workforce health is conceptualized within HPH&HS, operationalized through standards and organizational processes, addressed through workforce-oriented interventions and outcomes, and shaped by organizational conditions influencing implementation. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and CINAHL Complete were searched for publications from 1986 to 2026. Of 323 records identified, 148 were screened after deduplication, 60 full texts were assessed, and 51 reports were included. Evidence was synthesized across four domains: conceptual foundations, standards and governance, workforce interventions and outcomes, and implementation conditions. Results: Workforce health emerged as an intrinsic HPH&HS dimension, with healthcare professionals positioned as both targets and agents of health promotion. Workforce health was increasingly formalized through HPH&HS standards, governance structures, and organizational processes. Leadership, resources, workforce participation, competencies, integration into routine practice, and supportive policy environments emerged as recurrent implementation conditions. Evidence addressed health behaviors, occupational health and safety, psychological well-being, and job satisfaction, as well as organizational culture and staff participation. However, the empirical evidence was predominantly cross-sectional and heterogeneous, with limited controlled or longitudinal research linking HPH&HS implementation to improved workforce health. Conclusions: HPH&HS provides a conceptual and organizational framework for workforce health promotion, but implementation evidence is stronger than evidence for direct and sustained health improvements. Future research should distinguish implementation outcomes, organizational or work-environment indicators, and workforce health outcomes using longitudinal and controlled designs.

Heart transplantation (HT) remains a critical treatment for patients with end-stage heart failure who remain unresponsive to optimized guideline-directed medical therapy. This review examines recent advancements in pre-, peri-, and post-transplant screening and management aimed at improving patient selection, transplant accessibility, and clinical outcomes. Pre-transplant strategies include comprehensive HT candidate evaluation, risk stratification, donor selection, allocation policies that priotize critically ill patients, and mechanical circulatory support (MCS) to stabilize patients awaiting transplantation. Peri-transplant advances focus on strategies to maintain hemodynamic stability, minimize ischemic injury, and maintain graft viability immediately after HT. Post-transplant management emphasizes individualized immunosuppressive regimens, cardiac allograft rejection surveillance, and the prevention and management of complications to improve graft survival and long-term patient outcomes. Despite substantial progress, significant challenges remain, particularly the shortage of suitable donor organs and the risk of immune-mediated graft rejection. Emerging approaches, including artificial intelligence, xenotransplantation, and regenerative medicine, offer promising opportunities to expand the donor pool, enhance clinical decision-making, and improve HT outcomes. This review examines the research that influences the current policies and practices involved in HT, featuring the pivotal findings as well as any shortcomings present among these studies. Ultimately, continued research and multidisciplinary collaboration in each phase of HT are essential to improve the short and long-term health outcomes of transplant candidates. By integrating established evidence-based practices with emerging technologies, clinicians may further improve equitable access, survival, and quality-of-life for patients with end-stage heart failure.

This study examines the evolution of help-giving behaviour among 80 non-governmental organisation (NGO) workers in Ibadan, focusing on factors that influenced their aid provision. The aim is to understand how intrinsic and extrinsic motivations, such as altruism, religious obligations, and organisational values, shaped the help-giving behaviour of NGO workers. A mixed-methods approach was employed, comprising quantitative data collected through surveys and qualitative data obtained from in-depth interviews with NGO leaders and field staff. The quantitative data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while thematic analysis was used for the qualitative data. The study found that altruism and religious obligations were the primary motivators for help-giving among NGO workers. These intrinsic motivations were often aligned with personal values and the organisational mission. Cultural values also played a role, although to a lesser extent, while financial incentives were acknowledged but not seen as primary motivators. Overall, intrinsic motivations were more influential than extrinsic rewards in fostering sustained engagement among NGO workers. The findings suggest that NGOs should focus on strengthening intrinsic motivators such as moral responsibility, empathy, and religious or cultural values to maintain staff engagement and commitment, especially during times of financial constraints. This could ensure that workers remain dedicated to their roles and that aid provision remains effective, even when resources are limited.

The era of multi-messenger astronomy, where gravitational waves, electromagnetic radiation, and neutrinos from the same cosmic event must be correlated across a global network of observatories within minutes, presents a fundamental research software engineering challenge: how do you give the astronomical community instant, programmatic situational awareness of thousands of telescopes worldwide? HEROIC (Hop Enabled Realtime Observatory Information and Coordination) is an open-source research software platform developed by the SCIMMA (Scalable Cyberinfrastructure to support Multi-Messenger Astrophysics) project to address precisely this problem. HEROIC provides a REST API and an interactive web interface for tracking telescope status, instrument capabilities, and telescope pointings in real time, across observatories that choose to register with the system. The platform organizes data in a four-level hierarchy (Observatory, Site, Telescope, Instrument) and stores all sky coordinates as PostGIS spatial fields, enabling sub-millisecond spatial queries such as identifying which telescopes have observed (or are planned to observe) a given sky coordinate, using pre-computed field-of-view polygon indexes rather than live geometry calculations. In this talk we present the architecture and design decisions behind HEROIC, with emphasis on the software engineering challenges specific to real-time astronomical coordination: spatial indexing strategies for sky coordinate queries, automated schedule ingestion at cadence, deployment of stateful scientific services on community cloud infrastructure, and the tradeoffs involved in building sustainable open-source tooling for a small but technically diverse scientific community. We also discuss lessons learned from maintaining a production system that bridges telescope control software, public alert brokers, and end-user astronomers, and outline the roadmap for future development including expanded multi-messenger event follow-up coordination features.

Serum protein electrophoresis (SPE) remains a central laboratory method for the detection and characterization of monoclonal gammopathies and other dysproteinemic patterns. Despite substantial analytical automation, interpretation still relies largely on graphical representation and expert visual assessment, making low-amplitude or borderline abnormalities particularly challenging. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine-learning (ML) and deep-learning (DL) approaches, has increasingly been applied to SPE, with high performance reported for automated recognition of established abnormalities, particularly M-proteins, i.e., monoclonal immunoglobulins or immunoglobulin fragments produced by clonal plasma cells. However, most models have been developed against predefined diagnostic targets and evaluated using expert interpretation, immunofixation, or immunotyping as reference standards. Improved recognition of known abnormalities should therefore not be equated with discovery of additional clinically meaningful information. Modern electrophoretic platforms generate machine-readable numerical signals that may preserve features not explicitly considered during routine graphical interpretation. This creates the possibility of extending AI-assisted SPE from conventional pattern recognition toward detection of low-amplitude, distributed, or sub-visual signal characteristics. Yet current literature has focused predominantly on algorithmic performance, while the validation pathway required to determine whether additional AI-detected features are biologically meaningful and clinically actionable remains insufficiently defined. Evidence is strongest for automated M-protein recognition, including low-amplitude abnormalities, whereas non-canonical systemic patterns, longitudinal signal analysis, and AI-assisted decomposition of therapeutic monoclonal antibody interference remain exploratory. This critical review addresses this translational gap by evaluating AI applications according to the nature of detected information, strength of supporting evidence, and proximity to clinical implementation. We propose a translational framework addressing four complementary domains: analytical validity, biological validity, clinical validity, and clinical utility. The evidence required in each domain depends on the intended claim and clinical use.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) provides students with rapid access to explanations, summaries, and suggested answers. For 15-year-old learners, this accessibility raises an important educational and behavioural question: under what circumstances does AI support meaningful engagement with challenging learning materials, and when might it reduce opportunities for independent cognitive effort? This paper reviews published research in behavioural science and selected findings from the OECD's PISA 2025 Results (Volume I), with particular emphasis on Uzbekistan. Cognitive-demand avoidance and cognitive offloading are employed as theoretical frameworks for interpreting patterns of AI use, while a clear distinction is maintained between these concepts and the variables directly measured by PISA. According to the OECD, 48.6% of students in Uzbekistan use AI chatbots at least once a week to support their learning, compared with the OECD average of 45.5%. Furthermore, 80.6% of students in Uzbekistan report learning at school how to evaluate AI-generated information, compared with an OECD average of 62.6% (OECD, 2026). These findings indicate that AI-assisted learning is already widespread among students. However, the reported figures do not establish how frequently students substitute AI-generated summaries for assigned reading materials or identify the motivations underlying individual decisions to use AI in this way. The paper argues that the educational implications of AI use depend on the nature of the cognitive tasks delegated to AI, the learner's objectives, and the extent to which AI-generated information is critically evaluated and integrated into independent learning. As the study relies on secondary sources and does not involve the analysis of individual-level student records or the collection of primary empirical data, the proposed explanations should be understood as theoretically informed interpretations rather than established causal relationships. The paper concludes that educational institutions should develop students' ability not only to use AI tools effectively but also to recognise when independent reading, source verification, and critical reasoning remain essential for meaningful learning.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents, such as Claude Code, are increasingly used for security auditing, with task-specific skills providing reusable vulnerability-analysis procedures. However, their effectiveness in detecting real vulnerabilities and the reasons for their failures remain unclear. We conduct the first large-scale empirical study of 37 security skills using Claude Code with four underlying LLMs on 100 real Linux kernel vulnerabilities across ten classes, totaling 14800 runs. We evaluate vulnerability detection at the function, statement, and vulnerability-class levels. Results show that 24.4 percent of runs locate the correct function, 18.3 percent identify both the function and responsible statement, and 15.7 percent correctly classify the vulnerability. Our failure analysis reveals limitations in evidence acquisition, state-relation reasoning, code interpretation, candidate verification, investigation coverage, and reporting. Based on these findings, we propose SKILL-SIF, a self-improving framework that iteratively evolves security skills by learning from missed vulnerabilities and failure patterns. We evolve five top-performing skills using the original benchmark and evaluate them on 100 previously unseen vulnerabilities. SKILL-SIF improves fully correct vulnerability detection by up to eight times (from 2 percent to 16 percent) on unseen vulnerabilities, while aggregate accuracy across four LLMs increases by 1.85 times (from 6.05 percent to 11.20 percent). These findings highlight the limitations of existing security skills and demonstrate the potential of failure-driven skill evolution to improve vulnerability detection in coding agents.

The educational value of artificial intelligence (AI) depends on technological capabilities and human–AI interaction. This is particularly relevant in interpreter training, which involves high cognitive demands, contextual decisions, and time-sensitive activities. This study examines how Human-Centred Artificial Intelligence (HCAI) principles can guide AI-assisted educational environments for interpreter training. Using Design Science Research (DSR), an environment integrating AI capabilities across the training cycle was developed and evaluated. Drawing on literature concerning Computer-Assisted Interpreting, HCAI, human–AI interaction, technology acceptance, and interpreting cognition, five design principles were derived: learner agency and human control, transparency and calibrated trust, protection of cognitive resources, contextualised assistance, and AI as a support for learning. A technology acceptance study involving 42 professional interpreters provided contextual evidence on technology use, adoption barriers, and professional practice, informing the specification of these principles. The principles were operationalised in the artefact, and its interaction design was examined through formative heuristic evaluation. Professional evidence therefore informs the design without establishing learner-centred validation or educational effectiveness. The contribution is a human-centred, professionally informed framework linking literature, contextual evidence, design requirements, and implementation to align AI capabilities with educational objectives and the cognitive and interactional demands of interpreter training through explicit and traceable design decisions.

documents.abstract: AIM: This study evaluated whether a human factors-driven, integrated, color-coded resuscitation system that combines equipment standardization and prefilled-medication cognitive aids improves workflow efficiency and accuracy compared with a conventional crash cart during simulated pediatric resuscitations. METHODS: A prospective, randomized, crossover simulation study was conducted with 28 health care professionals. Each team participated in 2 pediatric resuscitation scenarios using either the SCC or the CCCC in random order. All sessions were video-recorded to measure equipment retrieval and medication preparation times. Statistical comparisons were made using paired statistical tests appropriate for crossover designs, with significance set at P<0.05. RESULTS: Use of the CCCC significantly reduced the time to locate airway devices (13.1±6.9 vs. 41.7±22 s, P<0.001) and airway adjuncts (13.8±11.9 vs. 30.8±17.4 s, P=0.03). Prefilled color-coded syringes significantly reduced medication preparation time (median: 16 vs. 19 s; absolute reduction 3 s, P=0.04), with no dosing errors observed. Teams using the CCCC demonstrated more consistent workflow and fewer procedural delays. CONCLUSIONS: In this randomized crossover simulation study, the integrated color-coded system reduced equipment retrieval and medication preparation times for selected pediatric resuscitation tasks. These findings are limited to the simulation setting and should be interpreted in light of the Broselow framework's use for both cart organization and assessment of correct equipment selection. Further research is needed to evaluate the feasibility of color-coded prefilled syringes and determine whether the observed workflow benefits translate to real-world pediatric patient care.

Abstract Shifting technological landscapes have been shaping the epistemologies, methods, and workflows of classicists, historians, and archaeologists for more than a century. Yet these technologies and their impacts have not always been subject to reflexive interrogation within our disciplines. As artificial intelligence (AI) technologies – especially generative AI – have become widely accessible, there has been a wave of concern among educators around student learning outcomes and academic honesty. In addressing these challenges, we must also engage in critical reflection around the use of AI technologies in our research and teaching from humanist and social scientist perspectives in order to serve critical learning outcomes and counter rising digital colonialism. This paper first situates the conversation within the context of corporate AI economies and the intersections between AI technologies and antiquity-focused fields. It then proposes three AI-focused literacies for cultivating core ancient Mediterranean studies competencies and fostering critical thinking: the ability to identify and analyse the impact of taxonomic frameworks and data training inputs on algorithmic outputs; the ability to understand the development of computational models and algorithmic reasoning and their applications; and the ability to critically evaluate the ethical and environmental impacts of algorithmic reasoning and AI technologies. Critical assessment of the foundational structures and logics of AI systems and economies situates both educators and learners to critically assess the political, social, and environmental impacts of such systems on the study of the past and the world in the present.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated creative exemplars are increasingly used as scalable digital instructional resources in creativity education. However, it remains unclear whether labeling identical exemplars as human- or AI-generated shapes how learners engage in group creative activities. We tested this possibility in 113 dyads using an fNIRS hyperscanning group creative ideation paradigm. Dyads completed creative ideation tasks before, during, and after exemplar-stimulation. During stimulation, the human- and AI-attribution groups received identical exemplars labeled as produced by human or AI, whereas the control group received no exemplar. Human attribution increased idea uniqueness during stimulation relative to both the other phases and the AI-attribution and control groups. AI attribution temporarily increased switching among ideation pathways. Neither behavioral effect persisted after exemplar withdrawal. The two attribution groups did not differ in exemplar-category overlap or nearest-exemplar semantic distance, but human-attribution dyads rated the exemplars as more helpful. Human attribution also increased interbrain synchronization (IBS) in bilateral premotor and supplementary motor cortices during stimulation, whereas AI attribution was associated with decreased IBS in the left supramarginal gyrus and right frontopolar cortex from pre- to post-stimulation. Thus, exemplar-source attribution shapes the process and outcome of group creative ideation, revealing an important social-contextual factor in AI-supported creativity education.

Data selection plays a central role in modern large language model training, as the quality of training data strongly influences downstream performance. A common approach is to curate a development set that encodes the desired skills (e.g., reasoning or multilinguality) and select data that are similar to them. Existing methods compute similarity using cosine distance over either the model's hidden states or gradients. However, we observe that this max-similarity strategy induces a mode-seeking bias: the selected data clusters tightly around the development samples. To address this, we propose ICLHerd, a data selection framework that leverages the von Mises-Fisher kernel to balance mode-seeking with mode-averaging. We further introduce in-context learning as a validation proxy, enabling efficient hyperparameter search over the balance trade-off. Results show that ICLHerd outperforms existing LLM data selection algorithms, highlighting the importance of balancing mode-seeking and mode-averaging.

Identity association under multi-source intermittent observations is a fundamental challenge in space object cataloging, space situational awareness, and complex measurement-data processing. To address the distortion of tracklet similarity caused by short arcs, weak observability, compounded errors, and interference from neighboring objects, a novel identity association method based on Cauchy-kernel semiparametric model optimization is proposed. First, through data modeling, identity association between intermittent measurement tracklets is formulated as a same-origin hypothesis testing problem based on measurable invariants. Second, heavy-tailed anomalous residuals are suppressed using a Cauchy-kernel loss, while systematic errors shared by measurement sources are compensated for using a semiparametric bias model, thereby yielding debiased measurable invariants. Then, the proportions of error components attributable to systematic bias, heavy-tailed anomalies, and quality degradation are adaptively estimated and propagated into an effective covariance to characterize the uncertainty of the measurable invariants. Furthermore, a profile-aware identity-consistency statistic is constructed to enhance the association capability for neighboring objects with different identities. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared with Euclidean-distance association, Mahalanobis-distance association, single-model gated association, maximum-correntropy interacting multiple-model methods, and kinematic-feature matching, the proposed method achieves superior identity-association performance.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence travel anchors are becoming influential in tourism live-streaming, but their persuasive mechanisms and user acceptance remain underexplored. This study develops a model grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model and Opinion Leader Theory to elucidate how these anchors shape travel intentions. After viewing live-streaming content with artificial intelligence anchors, 354 participants completed a survey, and the data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling to test hypotheses. The findings reveal that the popularity, professionalism, homogeneity, and interactivity of artificial intelligence anchors influence travel intention through the mediators of perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. These findings advance the understanding of artificial intelligence anchor applications and guide tourism enterprises aiming to boost tourist engagement and economic returns.

Research software supports scientific discovery through data analysis, simulation, modeling, and other computational activities. Defects in research software can affect the validity and reproducibility of scientific results. Peer code review can help identify such defects and improve software quality, maintainability, and reliability. However, research software engineers (RSEs) often conduct reviews with limited reviewer availability, small teams, specialized scientific requirements, incomplete documentation, and competing research responsibilities. This poster presents three connected studies that investigate peer code review in research software. The first study surveyed 61 RSEs to characterize their review practices, perceived benefits, challenges, and desired improvements. Participants associated code review with improved code quality, knowledge sharing, bug detection, performance analysis, maintainability, and technical debt reduction. They also identified time constraints, administrative and cultural barriers, small teams, limited domain knowledge, and insufficiently formalized review processes. The second study used semi-structured interviews with 20 RSEs to examine how research software teams implement code review improvements and what limits their sustained adoption. Participants described limited reviewer capacity, time pressure, gaps in Git and software engineering skills, informal review standards, and difficulties establishing supportive review cultures. They recommended lightweight pull-request workflows, automated continuous-integration checks, review templates and checklists, clearer expectations, mentorship, and greater recognition of review work. The third study investigates the use of AI-powered code review agents in real-world research software pull requests on GitHub. It examines the types of coding issues AI agents identify, including correctness, performance, security, and maintainability concerns. The study also analyzes subsequent code changes and pull-request discussions to determine whether and how developers act on AI-generated review comments. Additionally, it investigates which comment characteristics are associated with developer actions and explores developers’ reported reasons for acting or not acting on these comments. Overall, the study aims to provide insights into the practical use and limitations of AI-powered code review agents in research software development. The poster will present the ongoing study design and solicit feedback from the research software engineering community. Together, these studies connect empirical evidence about current practices and implementation barriers with an investigation of AI-powered code review in real-world research software development. The findings aim to improve our understanding of how AI-powered code review agents can support peer code review in research software.

documents.abstract: Hate speech detection in online environments poses significant challenges due to the nuanced and evolving nature of hate speech and the complexities of real-time communication. This study evaluates whether zero-shot large language models (LLMs), including Claude, Gemini 2.0, ChatGPT-o1, and ChatGPT-4o, can support the annotation of gaming-specific hate speech. We compare individual models, a multi-model collective, and TF-IDF–Logistic Regression classifier against an operational human-majority reference on 1,178 Dota 2 chat messages. We also examine whether ChatGPT-generated messages improve the traditional classifier when used exclusively as training-time augmentation, with full-archive augmentation and SMOTE as comparators. Among the automated approaches, the four-model collective achieved the highest accuracy and macro-F1 but did not uniformly outperform the strongest individual LLMs. For the class-sensitive measures, synthetic-data composition mattered more than volume. A post-hoc qualitative analysis identified recurring disagreement patterns and model-specific difficulties. Targeted augmentation achieved higher accuracy than SMOTE. The findings show that class-aware LLM generation can provide a competitive alternative to feature-space oversampling for lightweight classifiers, while zero-shot LLMs are best positioned as complementary annotation tools under human oversight.

Automated essay scoring (AES) using large language models (LLMs) offers promising use cases for language assessment, yet high-stakes testing requires scores that are both controllable and verifiable, which current LLM-based scorers lack. Given that, we investigate whether LLM-based scorers form distinct internal representations for individual scoring rubrics and whether these representations can be independently controlled. Probing and steering 25 open-weight base LLMs (0.13B-10.31B parameters; 14 families) on human-scored BESTEP English writing tasks, we find that holistic scores are decodable from model activations for the longer tasks (Parts 2 and 3) and only weakly for the shortest (Part 1). Furthermore, scoring rubrics have partly separable directions in representation space for the longer tasks, though not for short responses (Part 1). However, causal steering reveals a critical limitation: applying a matching intervention (e.g., steering "grammar" on a grammar-degraded response) yields only a negligible advantage (about 2% of the effect) over a mismatched intervention (e.g., steering "vocabulary"), and none that is detectable in any of the 10 testable comparisons across reliably measured rubrics. Rather than controlling distinct evaluative dimensions, the rubric directions share a dominant lever whose rubric-specific parts are not selective, which may mirror the halo structure of human ratings. Our contributions are two-fold. First, we show that analytic scoring rubrics designed for human raters do not behave as independent controls in base LLMs, even among the seven models whose scores agree best with human raters ($r \geq 0.6$). Second, we establish a methodology that shows that score agreement and decodability do not imply rubric-level control in LLM-based assessment.

LLMs are increasingly used across research workflows, including research ideation, qualitative analysis, and participant simulation. Within work on participant simulation, prior studies have largely evaluated simulated participants by how realistic or human-like their responses appear, leaving less known about how researchers use and critique these materials when revising interview protocols before fieldwork. We present Rehearsim, an inspectable research probe that treats LLM-simulated participants as materials for methodological rehearsal rather than substitutes for human participants. Rehearsim combines literature-grounded participant construction, interactive interview rehearsal, and traceable thematic review while keeping protocol decisions under researcher control. In a study with 21 qualitative researchers, participants used simulated materials to surface assumptions and gaps, reconsider participant populations, revise target populations, and develop follow-up probes. They also identified risks, including the concealment of weak questions, dismissal of unexpected synthetic details, and interpretive anchoring from generated themes. We derive an inspectable-rehearsal framework emphasizing traceability, contestability, researcher control, and epistemic boundaries.

Relevance. Tailing storage facilities (TSFs) are among the most accident-prone hydraulic structures in the mining industry, with a reported average failure-rate estimate of approximately 1.2%, while independent cumulative estimates range from 1.2% to 4.4% depending on the assumed global TSF inventory—nearly 120 times higher than that of traditional large reservoir facilities. Collapse of such structures is accompanied by catastrophic environmental and socioeconomic consequences, which underscore the need to improve monitoring and early-warning systems. Goal. A systematic analysis of current technologies for monitoring deformations in ground dams of TSFs, a quantitative assessment of their capabilities and limitations, and development of a conceptual architecture for an integrated geospatial monitoring system. Methods. A systematic review was conducted for 129 publications (2017–2026) discussing monitoring methods (GNSS, InSAR, SBAS, PS-InSAR, GB-InSAR, UAV, LiDAR, geotechnical sensors, geophysics), data integration technologies, AI/ML forecasting, digital twins, and early-warning systems. Results. It has been determined that no isolated method on its own provides complete monitoring of the structure’s condition: GNSS data are localized; InSAR loses coherence when deformations exceed 15 cm/year; UAVs are weather-dependent; and geotechnical sensors are point-based. Individual studies report reductions in estimation uncertainty of approximately 20–50% when complementary monitoring sources are integrated. Individual studies also report reductions in EWS response time and extended forecast lead times, but these values are heterogeneous and are not pooled in the present review. In one case study, a hybrid FEM–ANN–LSTM model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.027 for forecasting the dimensionless factor of safety (FoS) compared with 0.081 for an SVM baseline. Key research gaps have been identified: lack of explainable AI, limited validation of digital twins, absence of standardization in data fusion, and the lack of integration of climate risks. Conclusions. Further improvements in TSF safety require a shift from a set of independent monitoring methods to an integrated geospatial system that combines satellite, ground-based, geotechnical, and geophysical data with artificial intelligence, digital twins, and smart decision support systems. An eight-level architecture for such a system has been proposed, along with three implementation scenarios (minimal, comprehensive, and intelligent) and a roadmap through 2035.

documents.abstract: Abstract Urology education must prepare learners to integrate anatomical visualization, diagnostic reasoning, technical performance, communication, and ethical judgment, often under restricted working hours and limited access to high-fidelity cases. This viewpoint argues that large language models (LLMs) and metaverse-related technologies should be integrated as complementary, supervised educational tools rather than treated as autonomous replacements for educators or clinical experience. LLMs can support cognitive apprenticeship, documentation practice, assessment, and communication simulations, whereas extended reality, cloud computing, and virtual digital humans can support spatial, procedural, and remote learning. Our aim is to articulate 3 key messages: first, the educational value of these technologies depends on alignment with defined urological competencies; second, implementation should proceed in stages from governed data infrastructure to intelligent interaction and immersive multimodal training; and third, educational effectiveness must be established through prospective evaluations of transfer to clinical performance, not through technical novelty alone. We emphasize the need for rigorous randomized controlled trials, identify requirements for haptic and biomechanical fidelity, and discuss hallucination, bias, privacy, accountability, and deskilling. The responsible future of intelligent urology education will therefore require collaboration among learners, educators, clinicians, engineers, ethicists, institutions, and professional bodies.

documents.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence systems in public security and criminal investigations has expanded the possibilities for data processing, identification of individuals, and the generation of inferences intended to guide state action. At the same time, the use of facial recognition technologies and predictive systems raises questions regarding their compatibility with the fundamental guarantees that limit the exercise of punitive power. This article analyzes the ethical and legal limits of the use of such technologies within criminal prosecution, with particular attention to the risks arising from false positives, algorithmic opacity, personal data processing, and the reproduction of biases and inequalities embedded in the data used by these systems. It also examines the impact of these practices on the rights to privacy and data protection, equality and non-discrimination, the presumption of innocence, and due process of law. Based on bibliographic and documentary research, the study seeks to discuss the extent to which artificial intelligence may be admitted as an auxiliary tool in investigative activities and which legal safeguards are necessary to ensure transparency, auditability, human oversight, and the possibility of challenging algorithmic outputs.

documents.abstract: Mechanical product design integrates functional reasoning, geometric modelling, assembly planning, and engineering validation, yet remains highly dependent on human expertise. Existing large language models lack the spatial reasoning and physical constraint awareness required for engineering-grade design, whereas task-specific neural networks perform well in localised geometric recognition but are restricted to narrowly defined and repetitive tasks. Here we show an Intelligent Generative Design framework that enables autonomous mechanical design from natural-language requirements through biologically inspired coordination of task-specific agents. Integrating multimodal engineering knowledge, the framework decomposes design tasks, performs engineering analysis, generates dimensionally accurate three-dimensional models, infers assembly constraints, and validates kinematic behaviour. Across diverse mechanical systems, the framework produces mechanically consistent designs and completes multi-component tasks beyond standalone large language models. Intelligent Generative Design establishes a framework for practical AI-assisted mechanical product development, with implications spanning intelligent manufacturing, rapid prototyping, and design space exploration within diverse industrial domains.

Long-horizon human-scene interaction requires coordinated spatial reasoning, physical feasibility, and the ability to recover from compounding execution errors. Text-driven motion models are largely scene-agnostic and lack closed-loop correction, while geometry-conditioned approaches depend on paired scene-motion training or explicit 3D preprocessing that limits generalization to novel layouts and open-vocabulary goals. We present InteractAgent, an agentic multimodal LLM system for long-horizon human-scene interaction that plans, executes, observes, and reflects in a closed loop, using a single MLLM as both planner and evaluator and a frozen MotionLLM as the executor. InteractAgent integrates Online Observation for step-wise recovery decisions (continue/redo/replan) and Memory-Augmented Reflection for multi-round plan refinement with adaptive stopping. On UniHSI, InteractAgent improves task success and reduces penetration compared with training-free baselines. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/InteractAgent.

Introduction. Occupational disease incidence is an integral indicator of the realized occupational risk and efficiency of prevention, the prognostic value of which strongly depends on data completeness and reliability. Yet, the current multi-stage and multi-channel Russian system for occupational disease registration reduces the completeness and trustworthiness of records and creates discrepancies between medical and insurance statistics.The purpose of the study is to improve the system for registering occupational disease cases in the Sverdlovsk Region by developing architecture of an interdepartmental registry for dynamic surveillance, analysis of effectiveness of treatment and rehabilitation, and evaluation of disease outcomes.Materials and Methods. The materials of the study included data from the Regional Registry of the Occupational Health Center at the Yekaterinburg Medical Research Center for Prophylaxis and Health Protection in Industrial Workers (Regional Registry), the Sverdlovsk Region Branch of the Social Fund of Russia (Social Fund), and health facilities of the Sverdlovsk Region. We analyzed the document flow and logistics between occupational health centers, health facilities, offices of the Federal Service for Surveillance on Consumer Rights Protection and Human Wellbeing (Rospotrebnadzor), and the Social Fund. We also compared data from the Regional Registry of confirmed occupational disease cases with those of the Social Fund and health facilities on insurance payments and followed-up patients with occupational diseases, respectively.Results. The current system for occupational disease surveillance is characterized by multiple registration points, fragmented data, a lack of end-to-end patient support, and limited interdepartmental feedback, all leading to significant statistical discrepancies.Limitations. The study is limited due to the lack of common formats and mandatory routing of data on occupational diseases between medical, insurance, and surveillance authorities.Conclusion. The development and setting up of a single interdepartmental registry will improve the completeness and reliability of statistics on occupational diseases, ensure continuous patient support from diagnosis to outcome assessment and rehabilitation, and create a basis for management decisions aimed at maintaining the labor potential of the working population.Compliance with ethical standards.
