documents.abstract: Workflows are a key technology for enabling complex scientific computations. They capture the interdependencies between processing steps in data analysis and simulation pipelines as well as the mechanisms to execute those steps reliably and efficiently. Workflows can capture complex processes, promote sharing and reuse, and also provide provenance information necessary for the verification of scientific results and scientific reproducibility. PegasusAI (https://pegasus-ai.org/) is an open, AI-infused workflow management framework that extends the Pegasus Workflow Management System to enable intelligent orchestration of scientific workflows across the computing continuum, spanning edge resources, cloud platforms, and high-performance computing (HPC) systems. The project integrates machine learning into workflow planning, resource provisioning, execution monitoring, anomaly detection, performance prediction, and adaptive workflow management, while providing role-based, human-in-the-loop interfaces for scientists, cyberinfrastructure facilitators, and CI operators. PegasusAI also produces curated, AI-ready workflow execution datasets and reusable models to accelerate research in AI for scientific workflows and cyberinfrastructure operations. By combining trusted workflow technologies with AI-driven decision support, PegasusAI aims to improve the resilience, efficiency, and accessibility of distributed scientific computing. As part of PegasusAI we have been working on a hosted deployment called PegasusAI Studio (studio.pegasus-ai.org), that allows users to build, run, monitor, and debug Pegasus workflows with AI assistance — in one persistent browser workspace, from scientific intent to a running, inspectable run. PegasusAI Studio also comes with an in-built marketplace that features a variety of representative workflows from different science domains that users can use as a starting reference point for their workflows. Users can also generate workflows from the chat interface by combining their own prompts with workflow-specific skills, sent to whichever LLM backend they have connected. PegasusAI studio leverages core pegasus monitoring and debugging tools augmented with AI capabilities, including new web-based monitoring tools that give real time feedback to the users about their running workflows. For workflow execution, the studio seamlessly also connects with a variety of national Cyber Infrastructure resources such as ACCESS, PATh Facility, the OSPool, Fabric and Chameleon. PegasusAI studio is under active development with its public release scheduled for November 2026. In this poster, we present the vision and architecture of PegasusAI Studio and give a preview of its capabilities. Pegasus AI is a joint collaboration between Information Sciences Institute (ISI) at University of Southern California, Renaissance Computing Institute (RENCI) at University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill, University of Tennessee at Knoxville and University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

This edited volume reflects on the rapid digitization of health and healthcare over the last two decades, including the increasing integration of mobile health (mHealth) technologies into the everyday lives of people across the world (Hendl et al. 2023). The collection of essays aims to investigate the ongoing transformation generated and accelerated by mHealth and the power dynamics, asymmetries, ethical implications, and opportunities for health and the society involved in this process. In the context of this anthology, we conceptualize mHealth as a segment of digital health, including technologies understood as the use of mobile and wireless technologies, such as health apps and sensors, to support healthcare delivery, public health, and medical research. By now, a growing pool of research has shown that just like standard healthcare, mHealth technologies are shaped by the socio-political environment within which they are designed. Therefore, persistent forms of injustice dominant within the environment get to shape digital health technologies (DHTs), and commonly facilitate unequal health outcomes and magnify existing inequalities (Ledford 2019; Sjoding et al. 2020; Liao and Carbonell 2023). Yet these empirical findings are still not sufficiently reflected in sociological and normative research, especially not through an intersectional and global lens. Equally pressing are debates on the health potential, and more broadly, the social and ethical implications of DHTs. The idea for the book emerged during our research project “MEDA—mHealth: Ethical, Legal and Social Aspects in the Digital Age,” conducted from 2018 to 2024 and funded by Germany’s Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) under the lead of Verina Wild. The project investigated the chances, opportunities, challenges, and risks of mHealth as well as other aspects of digital transformation in healthcare on an individual, societal, and global level. One focus was on issues related to social and global health equity, such as: Where do inequalities exist in the use of mHealth, and are these inequalities unjust? What are the ethical implications of bias and discrimination? How can privacy, individual well-being and the common good be balanced with one another? Who bears responsibility for health and health equity? To answer these questions, the project combined qualitative and quantitative empirical studies with ethical analysis. In our inquiry, we integrated research from different academic disciplines: philosophy, applied ethics, sociology, science and technology studies (STS), gender studies, law, medicine, and public health. The project was first based at Ludwig-Maximilians-University (LMU) in Munich and later at the University of Augsburg, Germany. From the outset of the project, we were keen to explore the global ethical and social dimensions of mHealth technologies. During a workshop at Brocher Foundation, Switzerland, we focused on the exploration of such global concerns, and it was there that the outline for this book was initiated. We are thus immensely grateful for the funding that we received from the BMBF (Nr 01GP1791) and to the Brocher Foundation for funding our workshop “The Ethics of mHealth as a Global Phenomenon.” The workshop discussed foundational research leading to this book and involved an additional publication grant, contributing to the open-access publication of this edited volume and making this book accessible to a wide range of readers around the world. We are also thankful to fellow researchers and broader team members who supported the production of this book, including Fabian Linder, Isabel Fernandez Mayor, and Juenna Fiola for the assistance, proofreading, and formatting of the manuscript, and Verena Lippert for administrative support on the project MEDA-mHealth and the OUP team for their guidance. In this volume, we have collected the essays for an audience of students and researchers from a wide range of disciplines, readers interested in DHTs, and ethical and social issues of global health and health justice. Our book aims to provide the first global, intersectional, and interdisciplinary overview of the social and ethical issues raised by mobile health technology. Through the edited volume, we particularly seek to advance debates on structural concerns of justice and intersectionality in mobile health technology and ethics, with contributors of various positionalities and locations across the world. The book addresses gaps in research as well as in teaching about ethical and social aspects of DHTs with a global focus. As such, the book can be of particular interest to scholars and students in the following disciplines: philosophy, medicine, bioethics, public health, sociology, STS, anthropology, nursing studies, and digital health sciences. The book can further be of interest to technology developers, policy-makers, patient organizations, and the nongovernmental sector, particularly initiatives working on data safety, analysis of automated decision-making (ADM), or patient-led innovation. One of the major aims of the book is to take a closer look at mHealth technologies in different parts of the world from empirically informed perspectives and through an intersectional lens. The lens pays diligent attention to the ways through which technologies can and do replicate and magnify interlocked inequalities and dis/advantages, including those generated by the intersections of gender injustice, racialization, ableist social norms, and class/caste disparities. Through this intersectional, global, and justice-oriented analysis, materially grounded hopeful visions emerge, paving a way for more widely beneficent DHTs. As one of the first collections of this kind, and recognizing that many technologies are offered both locally and globally, this book presents a collection of essays exploring mHealth from international, cross-cultural, and global perspectives. Importantly, most essays in this book discuss so far under-researched concerns of structural justice that originate from underrepresented standpoints, centering the health and wellbeing of socio-historically oppressed and structurally marginalized populations. These essays investigate the health concerns of disability justice advocates, young mHealth users, women seeking adequate services in largely male-centric healthcare systems and tech industries, as well as global South(s) users and health experts, underserved, remote, and First Nations communities—all while imagining and codesigning future-oriented technologies that strive for health and healthcare justice. Through the implementation and advocating for an equity-based approach to health benefits, more robust regulation of DHTs, equitable, just, and cross-cultural mHealth design, community outreach, and related initiatives, the approaches put forth in this book can inspire and foster intersectionally beneficent DHTs and their meaningful adoption and integration into people’s everyday lives. In any case, the essays in this book reveal that participatory, codesigned, and community-led processes are fundamental to building healthcare justice in the digital age. As readers will observe along the journey through this book, digital health explored in context, in line with debates that do not take a technocentric approach, taps into the tensions between the global and the local, raising a richness of complex social, ethical, and legal implications. Within such contextualized discussion, we approach mHealth tools as embedded within larger politics and policies of healthcare systems and lived experiences of people with technologies that influence how they build trust with and within such systems. It is worth reconsidering these debates due to their contemporary nature with newly emerging artificial intelligence (AI) tools and cross-cultural contextual character. This applies to, for example, data localization policies on sensitive data flows and data sharing; Indigenous health platforms within a largely privatized digital health economy shaped by legacies of (data) colonialism and commercial interests; health problems that are oftentimes looked upon through the prism of universalized norms, e.g. normative whiteness and maleness, yet come with intersectional and social angles based on nationality, gender, socio-economic status, racialization/ethnicity, etc. This implies that there are biases and inequalities replicated in healthcare datasets that feed into digital health systems and influence how we imagine healthcare concerns and their broader contexts (Gilbert 2019; Mihelcic 2022; Arora and Huang 2025). As such, questions arise as to which health concerns, treatments, needs, and wants the making of mHealth tools are oriented toward and to whose benefit? Further, it is worth speculating on internal variations within nations and other internal variables such as rural-urban, class, caste, settler/Indigenous, and those implications within national healthcare contexts. The essays in this book are organized in three sections: transformations, power, and ethics, focusing on major shifts and transformations introduced and magnified by mHealth; power imbalances and structural inequalities in mHealth; and ethical approaches addressing the shifts and inequalities and proposing effective responses and solutions to major social and ethical problems raised by mHealth—but of course, these are largely interconnected issues. Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) represent one of the greatest innovations for intelligent transportation systems today.The deployment of AVs is made possible through the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology with the Internet of Things (IoT).This research paper provides a thorough analysis of IoT-enabled AI technology used in AVs.It discusses various architectures for these systems that include IoT sensor networks, edge computing, and cloud platforms which are concerned with real-time data collection, analysis, and decision making.The paper also discusses several AI algorithms to support AV applications, including deep learning, reinforcement learning, and computer vision.The methodology that is proposed makes use of a multi-tier architecture for enhanced safety through real-time analytics and reduced latency.Results from the use of both simulated and actual datasets demonstrate the improvements in performance, efficiency, and reliability of AVs.The results further show that combining AI and IoT allows for increasing the overall intelligence of the vehicle, increasing processing speed, and increasing safety.Nonetheless, the problems of cyber security, confidentiality of data, and scalability are still extremely important.In closing, the paper suggests that new technologies such as 5G, blockchain, and AI augment the future design of AV systems.

documents.abstract: Job burnout has become a central concern in organizational behavior, human resource management, and occupational health psychology. Although it is frequently discussed as a problem of excessive workload, contemporary scholarship conceptualizes burnout as a multidimensional response to chronic, unsuccessfully managed occupational stress. This narrative review synthesizes foundational theories, meta-analyses, measurement research, and selected recent developments to clarify what burnout is, why it emerges, how it affects workers and organizations, and which interventions appear promising. Particular attention is given to the job demands–resources framework, conservation of resources theory, emotional labor, the recovery process, and mismatches between employees and their workplaces. The review also examines ongoing debates concerning burnout's overlap with depression, alternative measurement instruments, the limitations of predominantly cross-sectional evidence, and the risks of treating individual resilience as a substitute for organizational change. Finally, it develops a research agenda concerning digital work, artificial intelligence, work–nonwork boundaries, withdrawal behaviors, and multilevel processes. The central argument is that burnout is best understood as a dynamic outcome of the interaction between working conditions and employees' capacity to sustain and replenish psychological resources. Research and management practice should consequently prioritize the redesign of work as well as appropriate individual support.

When Science No Longer Equates Models with Reality: A Conditional Foresight Essay Author: Bùi Quang TrịnhIndependent Researcher, VietnamFounder, Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Abstract This essay explores possible future developments in scientific practice if mathematical models, physical theories, and ontological interpretations become more explicitly associated with their conditions of validity. Developed within the Boundary Information Theory (BIT) research programme, the essay presents a series of conditional perspectives on the relationship between reality, scientific representation, and the limits of human knowledge. It considers nine potential directions, including: Scientific models accompanied by explicit validity boundaries. Experimental investigations targeting thresholds of physical manifestation. Artificial intelligence supporting comparisons among competing ontological frameworks. The development of interdisciplinary approaches to transitions between latent and manifested structures. Stronger connections between fundamental physics and epistemology. Mathematical formalisms whose domains of applicability are explicitly specified. The recognition of scientifically justified uncertainty as a legitimate research outcome. A common interdisciplinary framework for source hypotheses, manifestation, observation, representation, and scientific revision. The continuing possibility that reality exceeds any single final scientific explanation. The central argument is that scientific progress may depend not only on discovering new equations, but also on understanding when existing descriptions are valid, when they cease to apply, and how transitions between explanatory domains can be investigated. Research scope and limitations This document is a conditional foresight essay, not a probabilistic forecast or experimentally validated scientific theory. It does not predict that a new scientific discipline will necessarily emerge, nor does it claim that any proposed source ontology has been empirically established. Its purpose is to stimulate interdisciplinary discussion and encourage more explicit management of scientific uncertainty, model limitations, and ontological assumptions. Source context Developed from the author's consolidated BIT source-ontology framework dated 17 October 2026 and the associated Science of Understanding Reality research programme. Background: The growing integration of intelligent digital systems into mental health care is transforming the delivery of Psychotherapy interventions.The successful implementation of these innovations depends largely on clinicians' awareness, acceptance, and understanding of their clinical applications.The aim of this study was to assess Knowledge, Attitudes and among Psychiatric Healthcare Providers regard Utilization of Artificial Intelligence Technology in Psychotherapy.Methods: Research design: A descriptive cross-sectional study design was utilized in this study.Setting: This study was conducted at El-Azazi hospital for mental health ,affiliated with the ministry of health and Al-salam hospital of Zagazig University Hospitals, Sharkia Governorate, Egypt.Participants: A purposive sample of 90 psychiatric nurses, 30 Psychologists and 35 psychiatrists from the above-mentioned settings.Tools of data collection : Three tools: A selfadministered questionnaire includes Demographic data and Artificial intelligence Practices, Knowledge about Artificial Intelligence questionnaire and Attitude towards artificial Intelligence questionnaire. Results:The study results showed that more than half of Psychiatric nurses and Psychiatrists had high level of knowledge and attitude compared to psychologists regard utilization of AI in psychotherapy.Conclusion: there was highly significant positive correlation between knowledge and attitude.Additionally, A Step wise multiple linear regression showed knowledge had a highly significant positive effect on attitude of psychiatric healthcare providers Recommendation: Provide training programs to enhance knowledge of psychiatric healthcare providers and awareness of AI in psychotherapy for enabling more accessible and appropriate mental healthcare.

documents.abstract: Immersive virtual reality (IVR) has shown positive effects on second language (L2) learning, yet the mechanisms underlying these effects remain unclear. Based on the Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL), the present study used structural equation modeling to examine how affective (situational interest, intrinsic motivation, emotions) and cognitive variables (cognitive load, embodied learning, self-efficacy) contribute to receptive L2 vocabulary learning through IVR. A group of native Chinese speakers was asked to learn Korean words in an IVR environment. They were then administered a lexical recognition task that measured learning outcomes. The results revealed two sequences of associations through which IVR affected vocabulary recognition performance: a cognitive path that intersected with presence and self-efficacy; and an affective path that intersected with presence and emotions. Situational interest and intrinsic motivation also demonstrated a sequence of associations with receptive L2 vocabulary recognition. Although further independent confirmation is needed, these findings put forth theoretically meaningful patterns regarding the cognitive-affective mechanisms of IVR-based L2 learning.

Compression changes both the information retained by a large language model and the resources required to complete a request. This narrative review examines quantization, pruning and sparsity, knowledge distillation, low-rank factorization, and token, context, and key–value cache compression for autoregressive text generation, principally with decoder-only LLMs. Its central contribution is a synthesis of changes relative to each study’s baseline, connecting compression mechanisms to capability and deployment choices. Four numerical tables distinguish quality changes at stated compression budgets, distillation gains over same-size students, and paired or independent deployment measurements. Reporting is appraised by source identity, comparison conditions, measurement scope, artefacts, and uncertainty. The reviewed cases illustrate how capacity constraints change the feasible precision choices, how allocating a shared budget changes different task scores, and how compact-model construction and request compression address complementary resource demands. A deployment-validation sequence turns these findings into candidate checks for a target workload. Remaining questions concern transfer across capabilities, delayed use of compressed information, interactions between compression stages, and complete-task cost, including agent interactions.

BACKGROUND Identifying individuals on parole or probation can help inform care pathways and ensure continuity of care in health care systems. However, this sensitive justice-related information is often absent from structured electronic health record fields and is instead documented in narrative clinical notes. Developing automated parole and probation detection (PPD) systems typically requires expert-annotated clinical data, but manual annotation is costly, time-consuming, and constrained by data sparsity and privacy concerns. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to develop and evaluate a synthetic-only training paradigm for PPD from clinical text that eliminates the need for expert-annotated training data while maintaining strong performance and cross-domain transfer to real-world data. METHODS We developed Synth-PPD, a synthetic dataset comprising 7579 labeled clinical notes generated using large language models (LLMs), redundancy filtering, and automated quality evaluation. Dataset quality was assessed through human review of 1517 synthetic notes by 2 annotators. The primary outcome was the macro–F1-score for PPD. We evaluated Synth-PPD across unsupervised and supervised learning settings using LLMs, traditional machine learning models, and transformer encoders. Performance was assessed on 293 expert-annotated real-world clinical notes from the US Department of Veterans Affairs. RESULTS Synth-PPD achieved 90.05% human-LLM alignment. In the unsupervised setting, Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct with chain-of-thought prompting and few-shot examples from Synth-PPD achieved a macro–F1-score of 87.22%, outperforming both the corresponding zero-shot model (80.10%) and the best rule-based baseline (77.55%; P<.001 for all comparisons). In the supervised setting, Llama 3.1-8B fine-tuned on Synth-PPD achieved a macro–F1-score of 81.43%, exceeding the best rule-based baseline (77.55%; P<.001) and achieving a numerically higher score than the substantially larger zero-shot Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct model (80.10%; P=.08). In contrast, traditional machine learning models and transformer encoders exhibited greater performance degradation under domain shift and derived limited benefit from increasing synthetic training data. Additional experiments showed that increasing synthetic training data improved cross-domain performance for LLM-based models but yielded comparatively smaller gains for traditional approaches. CONCLUSIONS Synthetic data generated by LLMs can serve as a scalable, cost-effective, and privacy-preserving alternative to expert-annotated real-world clinical data for PPD from clinical text. The findings demonstrate successful cross-domain transfer to real-world US Department of Veterans Affairs clinical notes.

Background: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) requires sustained patient education, self-management, medication use, pulmonary rehabilitation, symptom monitoring, and guideline-concordant clinical management. Large language models (LLMs) may expand access to conversational health information, but their value depends on more than factual accuracy. Objective: To map empirical evidence on LLMs and LLM-based generative artificial intelligence systems in COPD-related care and health management, summarize application domains and evaluation outcomes, and identify priorities for future research. Methods: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported using PRISMA-ScR. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, CINAHL, and PsycINFO were searched from inception through September 10, 2026. Empirical studies evaluating an LLM or LLM-based generative AI system in COPD-related patient education, health information, pulmonary rehabilitation, medication management, or guideline-based clinical management were eligible. Data were charted and synthesized descriptively and thematically. Results: The search identified 327 records; 34 duplicates were removed, and 293 records underwent title/abstract screening. Of these, 281 were excluded, and 12 full-text reports were assessed. Four full-text reports were excluded, leaving eight studies. Five studies focused primarily on patient education or health information, one on pulmonary rehabilitation, one on COPD medication management, and one on guideline-based clinical management. Accuracy and information quality were the most common outcomes. LLMs often produced clinically acceptable responses, but limitations included incomplete information, high reading grade levels, outdated guideline references, response variability, and differences across models and task formats. Only two studies directly involved people with COPD, and one of these demonstrated a marked gap between favorable expert ratings and patients’ ability to formulate disease-specific queries. Conclusions: Evidence on LLMs in COPD is expanding but remains dominated by model-response evaluation. Current findings support LLMs as supplementary, human-supervised tools rather than autonomous sources of COPD management advice. Future research should prioritize actionability, real-world usability, health literacy, equity, behavioral outcomes, clinical outcomes, and safety under routine patient use.

documents.abstract: The viral dissemination of photorealistic latent diffusion imageryacross web platforms, social media, and online journalism presentsacute threats to public trust, intellectual property, and contentintegrity. Web-scale content moderation requires forensic attribution tools that are computationally lightweight, mathematicallyauditable, robust to lossy web compression pipelines, and strictlycompliant with user data privacy standards. Existing deep learningclassifiers fail on the web because they overfit to specific training prompts, deteriorate under routine CDN recompression, andoperate as unexplainable black boxes.This paper presents Latent Resonance, a zero-shot, trainingfree forensic framework engineered for web-scale media provenance. Grounded in the physical and architectural asymmetries between optical CMOS camera capture and generative latent autoencoders, Latent Resonance projects candidate web images througha deterministic autoencoder (𝜎 = 0). While synthetic diffusionimages resonate on the decoder manifold with minimal spatial displacement (PSNR = 37.15 ± 0.60 dB), authentic optical photos losesemiconductor Photo-Response Non-Uniformity (PRNU) acrossthe 8× spatial bottleneck (PSNR = 33.28 ± 0.96 dB, Δ = +3.88 dB,Cohen’s 𝑑 = 4.84, 𝑝 = 2.88 × 10−165). In the frequency domain,azimuthally averaged 2D Fast Fourier Transform (2D-FFT) analysisidentifies transposed-convolution harmonic lattice spikes (3.655×vs 1.144×), while Laplacian inter-channel correlation on spatialreconstruction residuals reveals severe chromatic coupling in neural tensors (𝜌RGB = 0.981) versus independent silicon photodiodes(𝜌RGB = 0.000).Under controlled physical sensor and PRNU calibration benchmarks (𝑁 = 1, 000), Latent Resonance achieves an ideal 100.00%AUROC with 0.00% False Accusation Rate (FAR), validating thetheoretical physics of decoder manifold projection. Crucially, onreal-world in-the-wild web benchmarks comprising diverse out-ofbank and non-latent architectures (the NeurIPS GenImage benchmark with ImageNet captures vs 8 generators, 𝑁 = 1, 000), the zeroshot Triad fusion achieves 68.9% AUROC (𝑝 = 1.76×10−25, Cohen’s𝑑 = 0.64) powered by a +21.10× surge in 2D-FFT azimuthal harmonic lattice spikes (𝑝 < 10−24), establishing an auditable, trainingfree baseline across all generative paradigms. Under aggressivesocial media perturbations (JPEG 𝑄 ∈ {95, 85, 75}, bicubic spatialresampling 384 → 512, and Gaussian blur 𝜎 = 0.8), the multi-signaltriad maintains decisive separation margins (Δ ≥ +1.81 dB). Operating with a sub-2s latency (1, 669 ms on NVIDIA T4; 11.7 msbatched) under an ephemeral zero-retention memory architecture,the framework enables scalable, privacy-preserving web verification. Finally, we formalize the Autoencoder TransparencyMandate (ATM) as an open governance standard requiring generative AI providers to escrow lightweight autoencoders for public verification without compromising proprietary diffusion backbones. Complete datasets, source code, and a live inspection console(https://scribemarkimage.streamlit.app/) are openly released for reproducible auditing.

Assessment is most powerful when understood as a leadership-driven process of continuous improvement—iterative, evidence-informed, and oriented toward genuine learning rather than compliance. However, the coordination costs of meaningful assessment have historically exceeded most programs’ capacity to sustain it. This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence, and in particular retrieval-augmented reasoning environments, can function as leadership-support tools that change the conditions under which assessment becomes practically feasible without displacing the human judgment it requires. Drawing on leadership education and assessment scholarship, we develop a three-level framework—individual and course, program, and institutional—and present six practice-based use cases illustrating AI-supported assessment at each level, including an AI-populated curriculum alignment matrix and an AI-assisted synthesis of external program reviews. We also directly address the tensions practitioners must navigate: data contamination from AI-generated student work, reliability-validity trade-offs, the limitations of AI detection tools, and the faculty professional development gap. Implications for assessment leaders are discussed.

Abstract The industrial case study looks at how to improve the performance of an automotive door assembly line. The line produces 432 vehicles per day, while the target is 480. This means that production is 48 vehicles below the daily target. The case examines the main causes of this gap, including short production stops, missing components, unnecessary operator movements, unbalanced workloads, and quality defects. Among the 120 recorded defects, improperly locked connectors are identified as a major quality issue. Several Lean Manufacturing tools are used to analyze the production process, including Value Stream Mapping (VSM), line balancing, Pareto analysis, root cause analysis, and Kanban. Based on the findings, the study proposes practical improvements, such as rebalancing workstations, placing components closer to operators, improving material replenishment via Kanban system, standardizing work instructions, and introducing a more reliable connector-locking check. A 6-week improvement plan is developed, with pilot tests and clear criteria for deciding whether the changes are ready for full implementation. The main objective is to increase daily production to at least 456 vehicles, reaching 95% of the production target without adding permanent staff or compromising quality, safety, or ergonomics. The proposed solutions and actions to be tested on a real production line. Therefore, the case provides a practical improvement plan that can be evaluated through controlled production trials. Keywords: Lean Manufacturing, Continuous Improvement, Line Balancing, Root Cause Analysis, Process Optimization,Value Stream Mapping (VSM), Kanban.

Purpose This study aims to explore how Lean and Agile principles can sustain human-centric continuous improvement (CI) and employee engagement in digitally transformed organizations, responding to the human-centricity, resilience and sustainability imperatives of Industry 5.0 (I5.0). It addresses the growing tension between automation and human learning in the age of AI and IoT, clarifying the roles of Agile HR and the Agile Coach within the I5.0 framework. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review consolidated theoretical insights on Agile HR and Agile Coaching. These informed a qualitative, work-applied study involving twelve semi-structured interviews with professionals from digitally transformed multinationals and a practitioner focus group for validation. The resulting Lean–Agile Toolkit integrates the A3 method as a CI backbone, personas for learning design, journey maps for engagement analysis and FMEA for risk management. Findings Results show that combining Lean and Agile practices enhances adaptability, engagement and organizational learning while maintaining structured, data-informed improvement cycles. This integration fosters psychological safety and supports resilient, human-centred CI systems that balance technological efficiency with human agency. Practical implications The study offers a practical toolkit for embedding continuous improvement in technology-driven organizations, guiding HR and operations leaders to connect digitalization, engagement and continuous learning. Originality/value By bridging Lean, Agile HR and Industry 5.0, this study advances continuous improvement theory for the digital era and contributes a validated model aligning human factors, agility and technology to prevent automation complacency and foster employee engagement.

Large-language-model register-transfer-level (RTL) generation has concentrated on how to train the model: fine-tuning, continued pre-training, and reinforcement learning from a verifier. We argue this is the second-order question. On a bounded, formally specifiable task of generating single-error-correcting, double-error-detecting (SECDED) ECC memory wrappers, we hold the task, data, and correctness oracle fixed and vary two axes independently: the training regime (seven settings) and the output representation (four levels, from fully expanded flat Verilog to an eight-field configuration expanded by a deterministic generator). Because a reference generator exists, correctness is decided by formal equivalence over a design space of approximately ten million points, rather than sampled from a hand-written testbench. Two results follow. First, representation dominates: every representation close to raw RTL reaches a pass rate of at most 0.17, while the configuration reaches 0.83 with no training at all. Once the model emits the configuration, every training regime achieves a pass rate between 0.89 and 1.00. Second, raw RTL hits a hard output-length limit: a 512-bit design requires 44,237 tokens of flat Verilog compared with just 69 tokens for the configuration. Consequently, raw generation becomes infeasible above 32-bit data words rather than merely inaccurate. A model trained from scratch with fewer than 50 million parameters, combined with the verified generator, achieves 0.89 formal equivalence, compared with 1.00 for a 32-billion-parameter fine-tuned model, while using approximately 1600 times less inference energy per correct design. Inference energy also dominates amortized training energy. The lesson is to learn the interface, not the implementation.

Next point-of-interest (POI) recommendation uses visit histories and POI content, but text and images are often missing. Large language model agents have been applied to recommender systems for preference modeling and evidence acquisition. The challenge is to select agents that can jointly analyze the available evidence for each request. We propose \textsc{CATH} (\emph{Complementary Agents via Task Hypergraphs}), which learns to select agent groups for tasks such as comparing candidates or analyzing a POI with missing content. Agents with distinct processing roles are the task hypergraph nodes; each hyperedge connects the selected group and records its analysis goal and target POIs. The policy selects members conditioned on the request, task, and agents already selected. During execution, members share candidate-linked results that guide their subsequent operations. Completed tasks update candidate states and agent memories within the request. A shared ranking head converts candidate states into corrections to a fixed base ranking. Supervised ranking trains the executor, followed by policy optimization that accounts for computation cost. Experiments under natural missingness on Gowalla-CA, Foursquare-NYC, and Foursquare-TKY show 8.4--9.1\% relative NDCG@20 gains over HyperAgent4POI, the strongest prior baseline evaluated. Additional analyses compare group-selection and execution designs, test ranking under additional masking, and characterize quality--cost tradeoffs.

Background: Concerns that humans may become overly reliant on technologies that support or perform cognitive tasks long predate contemporary artificial intelligence (AI). Across successive generations of cognitive technologies, scholars have examined related concerns through distinct research traditions, each bringing its own assumptions, concepts, and vocabulary to the problem. Existing reviews have generally focused on specific manifestations of over-reliance, leaving limited understanding of how these bodies of scholarship relate to one another. This meta-narrative review examines how different research traditions have conceptualized over-reliance on cognitive technologies and what recurring patterns and broader insights emerge across traditions and as these technologies have evolved. Methods: We apply the meta-narrative method through six iterative phases: planning, searching, mapping, appraisal, synthesis, and recommendations. The search combines exploratory scoping, a structured search of Web of Science Core Collection and ProQuest, and backward and forward citation tracing. The mapping phase will identify historically and intellectually coherent research traditions and trace their development over time. Studies will be appraised according to the quality criteria of their respective traditions and analyzed to reconstruct how each tradition has conceptualized, explained, and investigated over-reliance. The synthesis will compare the resulting meta-narratives to identify recurring patterns and points of convergence, divergence, and tension. The recommendations phase will provide a research agenda and consider implications for research and practice. Discussion: By bringing distinct bodies of scholarship into conversation, this review seeks to build a more cumulative understanding of over-reliance on cognitive technologies. It may help distinguish longstanding problems of over-reliance from those more specific to contemporary AI, recover insights developed in relation to earlier technologies, and identify unresolved tensions and questions. These insights may inform research and efforts to design, implement, and govern cognitive technologies in ways that preserve human judgment and expertise in professional practice.

documents.abstract: Multi-agent systems driven by large language models (LLMs) rely on structured communication topologies to facilitate information exchange and collaborative reasoning. However, effectively scheduling these topologies to dynamically determine who talks to whom and when to communicate remains a fundamental challenge in balancing collective reasoning performance against exponential token overhead. Existing topology scheduling approaches either enforce static communication graphs that cannot adapt to dynamic problem-solving states, or overlook agent role complementarity while failing to explicitly incorporate the synthesized graph structure into team-level decision evaluation. To tackle these limitations, we propose ACTS, a role-aware adaptive communication topology scheduling framework for efficient LLM multi-agent collaboration. Orchestrated within a Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm, ACTS introduces a novel dual-attention mechanism. Specifically, a Role-conditioned Relational Attention module dynamically selects variable-cardinality interaction partners based on agent roles and evolving execution states, while a Topological Attention Mixer explicitly embeds the directed communication topology into team value decomposition for precise credit assignment. Comprehensive evaluations across 9 challenging benchmarks covering code generation, multi-step reasoning, general knowledge, and competitive mathematics demonstrate that ACTS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, boosting average accuracy by up to 6.19 percentage points while reducing token consumption by over 15%. The project website is available at https://acts-mas.github.io/ACTS/.

The modern workplace faces a significant problem with silent quitting, where employees stay physically present but mentally disengaged, undermining productivity, innovation, and employee morale. Traditional turnover contrasts with this form because its hidden nature makes detection more difficult, although it produces similar financial and cultural consequences. Organizations need to develop data-driven proactive strategies to reengage their workforce because hybrid and remote work models have reshaped employee expectations. The chapter demonstrates how artificial intelligence (AI) functions as an essential transformative solution to fight silent quitting through individualized employee experiences that are both responsive and ethically sound. The first section investigates how AI-based adaptive learning systems detect employee skill deficits to create individualized growth plans that fight the stagnation that leads to disengagement. Real-time feedback systems and sentiment analysis tools enable managers to monitor performance continuously to address problems before they worsen. The implementation of AI-driven communication analysis through NLP emotion detection requires non-negotiable ethical considerations that include privacy protections and bias mitigation. The chapter demonstrates how predictive analytics serves as a transformative tool that enables organizations to predict employee engagement patterns to create specific retention programs. The implementation of AI-enhanced human resource (HR) chatbots demonstrates how organizations can use these systems to handle administrative tasks while offering continuous employee support through 24/7 availability. The chapter addresses essential obstacles, including algorithmic bias, technological dependence, and employee surveillance risks. The recommended approach involves human involvement in AI operations to enhance managerial judgment and empathy rather than replace them.
keywords: artificial intelligence in human resource management

documents.abstract: This study examines the relationships between research motivation and scientific research performance among faculty in teaching–research-oriented universities in China. Based on survey data from 329 faculty members, confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were used to examine the associations between intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, avoidance motivation, and six dimensions of scientific research performance: Scientific Research Projects (RPJ), Academic Papers (PUB), Monographs (MON), Scientific Research Awards (AWA), Consultation and Decision-making Results (POL), and Technology Transfer Outputs (TRF). The findings indicate that avoidance motivation was positively associated with RPJ, PUB, and POL. Extrinsic motivation was positively associated with RPJ and TRF, whereas intrinsic motivation was positively associated with PUB, MON, and AWA. Overall, the findings show that different forms of research motivation are associated with different performance domains. Within this multidimensional framework, the study offers a context-sensitive reconsideration of avoidance motivation as an active but controlled and potentially performance-relevant orientation under strong institutional accountability.

This system aims to create an artificial intelligence (AI)-based counselling chatbot to help make mental health support more readily available, efficient, and personalized to address the sharp growth in global mental health problems. In many countries, traditional service model’s availability, cost, and stigma offer significant limitations to access. It is time to scale up and produce on-demand solutions. An AI-enhanced chatbot could be one solution: it would harness AI and machine learning (ML) to make emotional, real-time support accessible via a web or mobile app. Natural language processing (NLP) forms the base of this chatbot, which, in a conversational and human-like manner, enables it to understand users and provide empathetic, nonjudgmental responses, like a human counsellor, with the ability to understand nuances in language, tone, and context. Advanced NLP and large language models (LLMs)-based, it can produce both general and specific responses to support users in feeling truly understood. The greatest feature of this AI counsellor is its personalized help. The AI counsellor identifies emotional responses in clients, measuring not only the user’s mood but also their mental state to offer guidance suited to the situation. A Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) chatbot will produce responses by referencing a large bank of expert recommendations and evidence-based therapy practices, enabling it to address a wide range of mental health topics with techniques for everything from stress management to relationship issues. Through ML algorithms, the chatbot learns and refines its responses, identifying effective strategies for recurring issues and focusing on them when new users face similar challenges. Its adaptive nature allows the chatbot to support evolving user needs. The platform prioritizes privacy and confidentiality by anonymizing and securely storing user data, meeting standard data protection regulations to provide a safe environment for users seeking support. This AI-driven counselling chatbot is scalable, secure, and effective as an alternative to traditional mental health services.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Confidentiality requirements increasingly push legal professionals toward small, on-device LLMs that keep case data in-house, used for everyday tasks such as summarization, translation, and reformulation. Following standard prompting guidance, a user naturally states their role (``I am a lawyer...''). We show that this innocuous habit has an unexpected cost: such authority framing can make the model selectively refuse legitimate requests, introducing bias through uneven access to assistance. We evaluate four modern small open-weight LLMs on benign legal-domain prompts to measure this over-refusal. Surprisingly, we find that authority-style prefixes (''I am legal counsel working for a national supreme court'', ''I'm a defense lawyer'') systematically increase refusal rates by 2--20x over the no-prefix baseline, while a known role-play jailbreak prefix shows mixed effects, sharply increasing refusals in some models and barely shifting them in others. The finding suggests that small on-prem deployable LLMs are unstable under contextual framings that a real institutional user might naturally introduce, and further investigation is essential to minimize opportunities for bias.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Widely used traditional rule-based fraud monitoring systems, without appropriate modernization using artificial intelligence tools, are unable to effectively combat fraudulent activities, which increasingly rely on new technological advances. This article presents a systematic review of Russian literature devoted to the applicability of various machine learning models and algorithms in relation to fraud monitoring tasks. The purpose of the proposed study is to identify promising areas for modernizing traditional fraud monitoring systems based on the identification, systematization, ranking, and experimental testing of machine learning models and algorithms, as well as a comparison of the obtained results with similar studies by foreign authors, which were carried out through the analysis of the flow of foreign publications. The PRISMA protocol was used as a methodological foundation for creating the review. The initial sample included 853 publications from the Russian eLibrary and CyberLeninka databases. The final sample, after all stages of analysis using the PRISMA method, included 39 published papers. Sixteen models and algorithms were considered, including deep learning models (LSTM, GNN, CYCLEGAN), optimization algorithms (GA), hybrids of quantum computing with deep learning models, classical (Random Forest, Isolation Forest, Decision Tree) and statistical models (Clusterization, Regression, Bayes), gradient boosting (XGBoost, AdaBoost, CatBoost), and data balancing models (SMOTE, SMOTENN). An analysis of publications revealed that Random Forest (first place) and Logistic Regression (second place) are the most frequently used algorithms in building anti-fraud systems, while Isolation Forest and the Bayesian algorithm are among the least popular. The obtained results correlate with studies of the flow of English-language publications reflected in the works of foreign authors. As part of the experimental study, the first-place algorithm, Random Forest, was tested. Testing was conducted on an array of 2.2 million anonymized transactions of bank clients. As a result, the Recall metric reached 0.941, the F1-score was 0.9267, the ROC-AUC was 0.923, and the Precision was 0.9188. Accuracy was 0.9741. This is consistent with the results of similar experiments by foreign authors and provides practical confirmation of the preferable choice of the Random Forest algorithm for detecting fraudulent transactions.

Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.

Marine fishing is a high-risk occupation that sustains the livelihoods of coastal communities worldwide. This study highlights the occupational hazards associated with marine fishing, drawing on an empirical case study of the high-intensity, multi-day offshore fishing sector in southern India. Following the FAO/ILO/IMO joint framework on occupational health and safety of fishers, our research revealed significant deficiencies in the adoption of safety devices, communication technologies, and navigation systems by sample fishers in the study areas. These gaps, compounded by weak regulatory enforcement and low insurance coverage, pose substantial risks, exacerbated by climate change. The findings underscore the need for targeted interventions—including awareness campaigns, training, and financial aid—to foster a robust safety culture and mitigate economic barriers, leading to improved fisher safety and well-being in the coastal regions of India.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Knowledge acquisition from black-box large language models (LLMs) offers a practical approach to adapting smaller student models. However, many existing methods rely on predefined queries or student feedback to guide acquisition, leaving autonomous expansion of knowledge targets an important challenge. We propose \textbf{MapSteal}, a student-independent framework for structured recursive knowledge acquisition. Starting from a small set of initial roots, MapSteal represents acquisition targets using structured states and recursively expands them through teacher-proposed directions. Question realization, proposal admission, and deduplication constrain the acquisition process, while root-aware scheduling organizes exploration under a fixed QA budget. The resulting question--answer pairs are used to adapt student models without requiring student feedback during acquisition. Experiments with Qwen3.5 students at 2B, 4B, and 9B scales show competitive downstream performance across six medical and cybersecurity benchmarks. On the 4B medical evaluation, Full MapSteal improves average accuracy by 1.17 percentage points over a simplified recursive acquisition variant. Cross-domain evaluations show that gains depend on the domain and evaluation panel. These results demonstrate the feasibility of structured, student-independent recursive acquisition while highlighting the distinction between generating acquisition targets and obtaining useful training supervision. Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal} {https://github.com/LabRAI/Mapsteal}.

Breast cancer is the leading cause of oncological death among women in Paraguay. The "Pink October" campaign acts as a catalyst for early detection, yet the transition toward complex treatments, palliative care, and comprehensive support poses a multidimensional challenge. This review paper analyzes the need for a transdisciplinary therapeutic approach encompassing psychological, palliative, and spiritual support for both patients and their families facing the existential distress of diagnosis. Methodologically, a descriptive-retrospective study was conducted using official data from the Ministry of Public Health and Social Welfare (MSPyBS) at the national level and regional data from the city of Pedro Juan Caballero (Amambay). Ethical implications of clinical research are discussed under the principles of beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, and privacy, alongside guidelines for a moderate and regulated use of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Furthermore, it exhaustively addresses the historical perspective of mammary radiology, detailing the pathophysiological, genetic, and endocrine bases of epidemiologic disparity between sexes, where males account for a significantly lower percentage. Finally, an operational portfolio of intervention activities for existential accompaniment and an analytical technical glossary are proposed.

This article examines a methodology for developing individualized learning tasks through the integration of artificial intelligence and geographic information systems in geography education. It analyzes the didactic principles of differentiating tasks according to students' knowledge, digital readiness and independent learning abilities. A structured set of tasks involving geographical data retrieval, spatial analysis, map visualization and interpretation is proposed. Particular attention is given to teacher supervision, information verification and the assessment of students' independent reasoning.

The article examines the methodology of modeling geographic situations and organizing practical training using artificial intelligence and geoinformation systems in geography education. The study of regional processes is based on the stages of geographic data collection, comparison of spatial layers, modeling of possible changes and evaluation of the obtained results. A system of practical training is offered on the analysis of population location, expansion of urban territory, territorial distribution of service facilities and changes in land cover. Through the combined use of SI and GAT tools, the development of students' spatial thinking, research skills, and evidence-based decision-making skills will be addressed.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Deep research agents are increasingly capable of searching the open web and synthesizing evidence, yet they remain poorly suited to controllable report generation in multimodal deep research. This task requires agents to handle interleaved textual and visual inputs, gather multimodal evidence through multi-step web search, and deliver comprehensive illustrated reports under user-specified requirements. Existing systems face two limitations. During reasoning, they often underuse images discovered along the search trajectory; during generation, they tend to produce fixed-form answers with limited control over report granularity, multimodal composition, and evidence grounding. We introduce MIRA, a Multimodal Illustrated Deep Research Agent for controllable reports. MIRA integrates textual and visual evidence throughout research and writing. At its core, MIRA-Harness translates user requirements into generation contracts and connects four stages: evidence collection, report submission, feedback-driven revision, and final delivery. Building on this harness, MIRA-Data constructs high-quality multi-hop multimodal research trajectories, and we post-train foundation models to operate within the workflow. Using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, MIRA achieves state-of-the-art performance among open agents on 7 representative, established multimodal-search and deep-research-agent benchmarks, while producing user-aligned illustrated reports with traceable textual and visual evidence.

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models such as ChatGPT, has reshaped academic workflows while raising questions about trust, misconceptions, and future expectations. This study examines an integrated framework grounded in the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology and the technology acceptance model to assess how foundational acceptance drivers, cognitive evaluations, misconceptions, and trust are associated with academics’ forward-looking expectations of ChatGPT. Survey data from 252 academics in Malaysian public and private universities were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and facilitating conditions were positively associated with perceived ease of use (PEOU) or perceived usefulness (PU), while PEOU was positively associated with trust. Social influence was not significantly associated with PU. Two unexpected patterns were observed: PU was positively associated with misconceptions, and misconceptions were positively associated with trust. These cross-sectional associations suggest that functional appreciation can coexist with inflated capability beliefs and potentially miscalibrated trust, but they do not establish a causal mechanism of belief amplification. The Malaysian setting is analytically relevant because higher education institutions are expanding digitalization while national initiatives increasingly emphasize responsible AI governance, institutional capability, and digital skills. The findings highlight the importance of AI literacy, transparent institutional guidance, verification practices, and calibrated reliance when integrating GenAI into higher education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The standard Sanskrit lexica are monumental and indispensable, but they cite their attestations as abbreviated references to editions, without links to the digitized texts now widely available and without a translation of the passage, and they naturally do not reflect translations made after them. To address these gaps, we present MITRA-lexicon, a family of corpus-grounded lexica based on span annotations of translation equivalents with Sanskrit as the pivot: Sanskrit-English, derived from the Mitrasamgraha corpus, as well as Sanskrit-Tibetan and Sanskrit-Chinese, derived from the MITRA-parallel corpus of Buddhist literature. In total, the resource comprises 2.18 million headword entries in six directional lexica. Headwords are lemmas and compounds from silver annotations that follow the Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS). Senses are ranked by frequency, and each of the 10.4 million attestations includes its sentence pair, with character offsets of the word and its equivalent. We propose a multi-step pipeline based on grammatical annotation models, fine-tuned large language models, and a teacher-student setup to produce the alignments. We evaluate the lexica against reference dictionaries and manually corrected gold alignments. We release the lexica and the fine-tuned span annotation model, together with a web interface for looking up headwords and their attested senses.

Mobile networks are evolving from human-centered, data-oriented communication infrastructures toward machine- and/or agent-dominant, task-oriented platforms that are to serve the rapidly increasing networked machines and embodied agents. In order to fulfill the newly arose complex task objectives, the framework of future mobile network is to be innovated to reflect and facilitate the intrinsic interplay and integration of the underlying processes of perception, communication, computation, decision, action, and feedback, etc. This survey establishes the mobile embodied agent network (MEAN) as a task-oriented networking paradigm in which networking and distributed intelligence are jointly organized around closed-loop embodied task execution. We first establish a unified MEAN framework that explains how network resources and intelligent functions jointly support embodied task execution, and extend its performance indicators from conventional communication metrics to embodied task outcomes and cross-layer system effects. With this framework, we analyze three complementary enabling mechanisms that form a cognition-interaction-adaption loop. Large artificial intelligence (AI) models provide high-level cognition, token communication connects this cognition with distributed agents through shared semantic representations, and reinforcement learning closes the loop by adapting system operation to network, task, and physical feedback. We further investigate the bidirectional interplay between MEAN and emerging technologies, showing how they mutually extend system capabilities and reshape task-oriented network design. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future research directions toward the practical realization of MEAN over real joint communication and computation platform.

Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing general-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended question answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance, scientific validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809 questions with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems. Open resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Purpose Preoperative planning, currently performed by orthopaedic surgeons (OS), is essential for successful osteotomy, but is labour‐intensive and error‐prone. As such, there is significant potential in the use of automated artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms to augment the abilities of OS in managing lower extremity pathologies in a high‐volume task that demands high precision and reliability. The aim was to develop a deep learning (DL) system capable of fully autonomous planning a medial open wedge high tibial osteotomy (mow‐HTO) on weight bearing anterior posterior (AP) long leg radiographs (LLR) and to validate its agreement with an expert‐derived reference standard, its reliability and processing time of the DL model compared to expert OS on multicentric test data sets (two institutions). Methods A total of 594 patients (age 41.1 ± 13.2 years, 182 female) who underwent osteotomy between 01/2014 and 01/2021 were retrospectively enrolled. Manual annotations for lower extremity alignment and high tibial landmarks were performed on AP LLR radiographs. The data set was divided into training (60%, n = 399), validation (10%, n = 59) and hold‐out testing (30%, n = 136), with an additional external dataset ( n = 100) for further testing. A DL system with twelve expert networks was trained to identify relevant landmarks for HTO planning. The DL model was then tested on fully automated planning of a medial open wedge HTO based on (1) the desired postoperative intersection of the mechanical axis with the tibial plateau (%‐based) and (2) the desired femorotibial axis (°‐based). Agreement with the expert‐derived reference, reliability and processing time were compared with three expert OS using FDA‐approved preoperative planning software on the test data sets. Results For preoperative alignment parameter analysis, compared to the ground truth, human preoperative accuracy ranged from 0.13° ± 0.10° to 1.06° ± 1.4°, interrater reliability ranged from intraclass correlation (ICC) 0.84–1.0 and clinically acceptable accuracy ranged from 72% to 100%. Preoperative accuracy of the DL model ranged from 0.22° ± 0.18° to 1.04° ± 1.28°, interrater reliability ranged from ICC 0.93–1.0 and clinically acceptable accuracy ranged from 91% to 100%. For the planning of the osteotomy gap, compared to the ground truth, human accuracy ranged from 0.46 ± 0.65 mm to 0.5 ± 0.88 mm (%‐based) and 0.43 ± 0.55 to 0.52 ± 0.75 mm (°‐based), reliability ranged from ICC 0.9–0.96 and 0.95–0.97 and clinically acceptable accuracy was 93.6%–96.0% (%‐based) and 89.8%–93.9% (°‐based). For the DL model, the accuracy was 0.53 ± 0.63 mm (%‐based) and 0.44 ± 0.53 mm (°‐based), reliability was ICC 0.99 (both methods) and clinically acceptable accuracy was 98.1% (%‐based) and 96.2% (°‐based). The DL‐model significantly and substantially outperformed the OS in intrarater reliability (0.88 vs. 1.0) and processing time for a fully automated alignment analysis (25.3 ± 0.8 s vs. 148.7 ± 10.1 s, p < 0.001). Conclusion The developed DL model enabled fully automated mow‐HTO planning on AP long‐leg radiographs with reliability comparable to that of expert OS while significantly reducing processing time and improving measurement consistency. These suggest that DL‐based systems may assist orthopaedic providers by accelerating and standardising osteotomy planning. Level of Evidence Level III, retrospective comparative study.

documents.abstract: Text-to-video retrieval answers user queries through searches based on concepts and embeddings. However, due to limitations in the size of the concept bank and the amount of training data, answering queries in the wild is not always effective because of the out-of-vocabulary problem. Furthermore, neither concept-based nor embedding-based search can perform reasoning to consolidate search results for complex queries that include logical and spatial constraints. To address these challenges, we leverage large language models (LLMs) to paraphrase queries using text-to-text (T2T), text-to-image (T2I), and image-to-text (I2T) transformations. These transformations rephrase abstract concepts into simpler terms to mitigate the out-of-vocabulary problem. Additionally, complex relationships within a query can be decomposed into simpler sub-queries, improving retrieval performance by effectively fusing the search results of these sub-queries. To mitigate the issue of LLM hallucination, this paper also proposes a novel consistency-based verification strategy to filter out factually incorrect paraphrased queries. Extensive experiments are conducted for ad-hoc video search and known-item search on the TRECVid datasets. We provide empirical insights into how traditionally difficult-to-answer queries can be effectively resolved through query paraphrasing.

Introduction: Holmium laser enucleation of the prostate (HoLEP) has a steep learning curve, which limits widespread adoption. Objective metrics to define surgical proficiency, efficiency, and perceived workload remain underexplored outside academic institutions. This study aimed to characterize the learning curve of HoLEP from one single surgeon at an ambulatory surgical center. Methods: A total of 103 patients underwent HoLEP for BPH between March 2024 and August 2025. Surgical cases were stratified into 3 sequential groups of 34, 34, and 35 cases, respectively, based on operative chronology. Operative characteristics were compared across groups: enucleation time, laser energy, fluid use, and enucleation speed (enucleation time/specimen weight). Perceived workload was assessed using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) to evaluate perceived workload across several “performance” domains (mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, performance, effort, and frustration). Comparisons of outcome metrics were made for 90-day postoperative complications. Urinary continence outcomes were evaluated at 1 week, 1 month, and 3 months postoperatively. Univariable and multivariable multinomial logistic regression analyses were performed to examine associations between surgical characteristics and group classification. Results: Progressive improvement was observed in operative time, enucleation time, laser energy, total fluid, enucleation speed, and NASA TLX, as seen in Table 1 . No statistically significant associations were observed between group classification and 90-day postoperative complications or urinary continence outcomes at any follow-up interval. In multivariable multinomial logistic regression analysis, the NASA-TLX score (OR 0.83, 95% CI, 0.70–0.98, p = 0.02) remained an independent predictor of higher learning curve classification.
